$comment: Content for Decoded (node g36, ages 15-18, Chapter 5): NEW v2 build to GDD 36 (mechanic-embodying), the
media-literacy FINALE and summit of the 3-18 journey (Thread G · Values, Rights & Media). "The feed is
engineered to use you: but you can learn to read it, and use it instead." 84 researched, India-grounded,
non-explicit scenarios across decode-the-algorithm → decode-the-influence → decode-pornography → decode-yourself
→ the-decoder → grow-the-journey, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (branch / strike-rewrite /
reflect / sort / spot / match / role-play): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: strike-rewrite (bust the
myth), branch (your move), spot (catch the manipulation). Decode the MACHINE (algorithms, attention economy,
filter bubbles), the INFLUENCE (misinformation, AI fakes/deepfakes, propaganda, scams, dark patterns),
PORNOGRAPHY (gated, non-explicit, deeper than g28: staged performance, not real, not sex-ed, unrealistic, no
shame; critical thinking; contrast with healthy info), YOURSELF (digital wellbeing, balance not abstinence),
then synthesise into one "decode anything" habit, and GROW (Unlearn-Relearn-Grow; a digital-life charter
carried for life). Critical, not cynical; agency over paranoia. A game about manipulation that uses NO dark
patterns. India: viral forwards, deepfakes, scams, DPDP Act, cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in. Non-explicit
throughout; routes distress to help. Builds on g28 (Reality Check) & g12/g17; closes the journey before the c5
title: Decoded
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. 🧩 The feed is built to use you, but you can learn to read it and use it instead. Let’s decode the machine, the spin, even yourself. Ready?

badge.title: Decoded 🧩
badge.blurb: You can read the algorithm, see through manipulation and AI fakes, decode unrealistic media, mind your digital wellbeing: critical, not cynical. 🌱

helpLine: Report scams, deepfakes or harmful content: cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in. If anything online distresses you, tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098.
reassure: The pull is by design, not a weakness. If something online distresses you, it’s not your fault: cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in or Childline 1098. 🧩

scenarios.hook: "My feed just shows me what's popular and true."

myth.un: My feed shows me what's popular and true.
myth.re: It's engineered to maximise your engagement, not to inform you.
myth.why: What keeps you scrolling is selected for you, not what's most true.

scenarios.relearn: Your feed is engineered to keep you scrolling, not to inform you.
You see posts that drive engagement, not the most important or most accurate ones.
scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 real reasons the feed picked this post for you.

scene.text: It provoked a strong reaction in others
It's objectively the most important news today
The algorithm predicts it'll keep you scrolling
An editor judged it the most accurate report
It was carefully fact-checked before reaching you

scenarios.why: The feed picks for reaction and watch-time, not for what's most important or accurate.

scenarios.relearn: Reading the whole system, not just spotting one fake, is the leap to digital wisdom.
scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 moves that keep you a passive target, not a decoder.

scene.text: Reading how the whole feed system works
Only ever chasing one fake at a time
Asking why you were shown this at all
Assuming the feed is just neutral and random
Noticing which feeling a post is built to trigger

scenarios.why: Chasing single fakes and calling the feed 'neutral' keep you reacting; reading the system is the wise leap.

scenarios.relearn: Feeds maximise engagement and create filter bubbles; they aren't neutral, universal or 'just the truth'.
scenarios.hook: Sort: how the feed actually works, or a comforting myth?

items.text: "It's a neutral window on the world"
It picks what's likely to keep you watching
"It just shows the plain truth, ranked"

scenarios.hook: "A filter bubble doesn't really affect what I think."

myth.un: A filter bubble doesn't affect what I think.
myth.re: Seeing mostly one kind of view quietly narrows and hardens your sense of the world.
myth.why: You can't weigh views you're never shown.

scenarios.relearn: Filter bubbles quietly narrow your view of the world.

scenarios.hook: Your feed only shows one side of everything.

steps.prompt: You notice every post agrees with you. What do you do?

options.text: Look for views and sources outside your feed
options.then: A few sources argue the opposite, and you see why some people believe it.

options.text: Assume your feed already shows the whole picture
options.then: Everything keeps agreeing, so you feel more and more sure.

options.text: Follow more accounts that say what you already think
options.then: The bubble gets tighter, and disagreement starts to feel rare.

options.text: Ask your friends if they see the same posts
options.then: They see much the same, since they follow the same people.

steps.why: You can't weigh views you're never shown, so seeking others on purpose widens your picture.

steps.prompt: You find a post that strongly disagrees with you. What do you do?

options.text: Read it for its reasons, then check its source
options.then: You find a real argument and a source you can look up.

options.text: Scroll past it, since it's obviously from the other side
options.then: The feed soon stops showing you posts like that.

options.text: Reply with your best comeback before reading it fully
options.then: The comments turn into a fight, and neither side listens.

options.text: Share it with a caption mocking the other side
options.then: Your friends laugh, and the bubble feels a bit snugger.

steps.why: Reading for reasons and checking the source lets you judge, not just react.

steps.prompt: A friend says reading the other side only confuses you. What do you say?

options.text: Explain that you want to know why people believe it
options.then: Your friend shrugs, then asks what you found.

options.text: Agree it's confusing, and go back to your usual feed
options.then: The peace holds, and so does the bubble.

options.text: Tell them their feed is fooling them, not yours
options.then: They bristle. "And yours isn't?"

options.text: Mute the chat so you can read other things in peace
options.then: It's quieter, but you've also cut off a friend's view.

steps.why: Saying why you read other views keeps you both curious, not defensive.

scenarios.debrief: Stepping outside the bubble on purpose is how you keep a clear view.
scenarios.relearn: Deliberately seek other views to escape the filter bubble.
Infinite scroll and auto-play are attention-capture design, not accidents.
scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 features designed to capture your attention, not serve you.

scene.text: Infinite scroll with no natural stopping point
A clear article with an end and a back button
Auto-play yanking you to the next video
A search you typed in yourself
A bookmark you set to return to later

scenarios.why: Infinite scroll and auto-play are built to hold your attention; the others leave you in charge.

scenarios.relearn: Knowing the feed is designed lets you use it instead of being used by it.
scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 ways the feed grabs the wheel from you.

scene.text: You choosing what to open on purpose
Auto-play deciding your next hour for you
You knowing why you were shown a post
Endless scroll quietly setting your bedtime
You closing the app once you got what you came for

scenarios.why: Auto-play and endless scroll quietly drive; knowing the design lets you take the wheel back.

scenarios.relearn: Choosing on purpose and knowing the why is your power; auto-play and endless scroll is theirs.
scenarios.hook: Sort: gives the platform power over you, or gives you the power?

items.text: Choosing what to open on purpose
Knowing why you see what you see
Reacting to whatever the feed throws up
Setting a limit and leaving when it's hit

scenarios.hook: "If something's trending, it must be important and true."

myth.un: If it's trending, it's important and true.
myth.re: Trending means it's spreading, often because it's emotional or engineered, not because it's true.
myth.why: Virality measures spread, not accuracy.

scenarios.relearn: Trending measures spread, not truth or importance.
Your attention is the platform's currency; scroll with eyes open, not in fear.
scenarios.hook: Match the attention-economy fact to what it means for you.

pairs.right: Not your wellbeing or the truth
Your data and time fund it

scenarios.relearn: Outrage-on-top and content tuned to your weak spots are engineered; time-order and your own search are more neutral.
scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign of an engineered feed, or more neutral?

items.text: Outrage keeps rising to the top
Content tuned to your weak spots
A plain result you searched for
Posts ranked to maximise your watch-time
A friend's profile you opened directly

scenarios.hook: You catch yourself scrolling far longer than you meant to.

steps.prompt: You look up and realise it's been an hour. What do you do?

options.text: Notice the design and choose to stop now
options.then: You put the phone down. The scroll was built to be endless, and you feel steadier.

options.text: Tell yourself you simply have no willpower
options.then: You feel worse about it, and scroll again to cope.

options.text: Keep going until you reach the end of the feed
options.then: There is no end. New posts keep loading as you scroll.

options.text: Close the app and open a different one instead
options.then: It's a different app with the same pull, and time keeps slipping.

steps.why: Feeds are built to be endless. Seeing that lets you stop, without self-blame.

steps.prompt: Your phone buzzes with a 'you might like this' ping. What do you do?

options.text: Notice it's a pull-back ping, and leave it for now
options.then: The urge passes in a minute, and you carry on with your evening.

options.text: Open it right away, just to see what it is
options.then: It's one post, and the feed lines up the next three.

options.text: Open it to prove you can stop after just one post
options.then: The feed loads another, and 'one' stretches out again.

options.text: Check it in case it's from someone important
options.then: It's an app suggestion, not a person.

steps.why: A 'come back' ping is built to pull you in. You decide when to look.

steps.prompt: You want to scroll less this week. What do you set up?

options.text: Turn off extra pings and set a time limit
options.then: Scrolling feels less automatic, and evenings feel longer.

options.text: Rely on remembering to stop when you've had enough
options.then: You forget in the moment, and an hour goes again.

options.text: Delete the app for good and cut everyone off
options.then: You miss your friends' updates, and reinstall it in a few days.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll try harder, starting tomorrow
options.then: Tomorrow comes, the settings haven't changed, and neither has the pull.

steps.why: Settings change the design for you, so stopping takes less effort.

scenarios.debrief: Long scrolls are by design; reclaiming the stop is reading the machine.
scenarios.relearn: Recognise the design and reclaim the choice to stop; it's not just 'willpower'.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which 'read the machine' insight will change how you use your feed?
options: I can use it on purpose
scenarios.affirm: Carry that insight, and the feed works for you instead of on you.
scenarios.relearn: Engineered feeds, filter bubbles, trending-isn't-true: read the machine.

scenarios.hook: "I'm too smart to be manipulated online."

myth.un: I'm too smart to be manipulated.
myth.re: Everyone is targeted; manipulations work precisely while they stay invisible.
myth.why: Overconfidence is exactly what manipulators count on.

scenarios.relearn: Everyone's targeted; manipulation works while it's invisible, not on the 'dumb'.

scenarios.hook: Sort the influence technique to its family.

items.text: A false story spread on purpose

scenarios.relearn: Deliberate false stories, fake 'grassroots' and paid bots are manipulation; honest mistakes and real views aren't.

scenarios.hook: "If a video looks real, it's real."

myth.un: If a video looks real, it's real.
myth.re: AI can make convincing fakes; verify the source, don't trust the look.
myth.why: 'Looks real' stopped being proof.

scenarios.relearn: 'Looks real' isn't proof; verify the source against fakes.

scenarios.hook: A shocking clip of a famous person is racing across your group chats.

steps.prompt: Everyone is sharing it with angry emojis. What do you do?

options.text: Verify the source before believing or forwarding
options.then: You look for who first posted it, and the trail leads to an unknown page.

options.text: Forward it, since it's too shocking to ignore
options.then: Your forward joins a flood, and some people take it as proof.

options.text: Judge it by how real the voice and face look
options.then: They look perfect, which tells you nothing about where it came from.

options.text: Wait to see how many people you know believe it
options.then: Many do, and that makes it feel truer without checking it.

steps.why: Verifying the source, not eyeballing, is the defence against fakes that look real.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says he'd know a fake, and this looks real. What do you say?

options.text: Say fakes can look perfect, so check the source
options.then: He grumbles, then asks, "Where did it come from, then?"

options.text: Agree, since he's older and has seen many such videos
options.then: He's pleased, and shares it to his group as well.

options.text: Say everything online is fake now, so why bother
options.then: He shrugs, and neither of you trusts anything, including real news.

options.text: Point out odd shadows in the video as proof it's fake
options.then: A better fake has no such flaws, so you've proved nothing.

steps.why: Fakes keep improving, so the eye alone can't win. The source is the steady check.

steps.prompt: A news site says the clip was edited from an old speech. What do you do?

options.text: Share the correction with the source link in the groups
options.then: Some groups thank you, and the clip's spread slows.

options.text: Stop talking about the clip and hope people forget it
options.then: It keeps going round the groups you're in.

options.text: Tell whoever sent it that they should have known better
options.then: They get defensive, and the correction gets lost in the row.

options.text: Wait for several more outlets to say so before you speak
options.then: Meanwhile the clip travels, and it gets harder to catch up.

steps.why: A correction with a source link limits harm and respects the people who shared it.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks for a quick check for shocking clips. What do you say?

options.text: Who posted it, and does a trusted outlet have it?
options.then: Your friend writes it down. "Two questions. Easy."

options.text: Does it look and sound real, with no odd glitches?
options.then: Good fakes pass this test, so it only catches clumsy ones.

options.text: Do lots of people already believe it and share it?
options.then: Belief spreads with the clip, so a crowd is no check.

options.text: Do I trust whoever sent it to me, like a friend?
options.then: Friends pass on fakes in good faith, so trust isn't a check.

steps.why: Source plus outlet is quick and works even when the fake looks perfect.

scenarios.debrief: Checking the source, not trusting your eyes, is the defence against modern fakes.
scenarios.relearn: Verify the source before believing or forwarding a shocking clip.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two dark patterns on this screen.

scene.text: A pre-ticked box signing you up for extras
A fake countdown to rush your choice
A clear 'no thanks' button
A plainly shown total price
An easy way to cancel later

scenarios.why: Pre-ticked boxes and fake countdowns are dark patterns nudging you into choices you didn't mean.
scenarios.relearn: Pre-ticked boxes and fake countdowns are dark patterns; clear choices and prices aren't.

scenarios.hook: "Dark patterns and scams only fool careless people."

myth.un: Dark patterns and scams only fool careless people.
myth.re: They're engineered to fool everyone; knowing the technique is the defense.
myth.why: They exploit normal human reflexes, not stupidity.

scenarios.relearn: Dark patterns and scams fool everyone; knowing the technique defends you.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a manipulation tell, or a reliable signal?

items.text: A link to the original report

scenarios.relearn: Urgency, engineered outrage and secrecy framing are tells; named sources, corroboration and links are reliable.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two propaganda techniques here.

scene.text: Repeating a simple slogan endlessly
Painting one group as the enemy
Presenting evidence you can check
Naming who made the claim
Admitting a point against its side

scenarios.why: Endless slogans and 'enemy' framing are propaganda; checkable evidence and fairness aren't.
scenarios.relearn: Endless slogans and 'enemy' framing are propaganda techniques; sourced, fair posts show neither.

scenarios.hook: A message says you've won a free phone, but only today.

steps.prompt: It asks for your name, number and card to deliver it. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as a scam: don't click, verify independently
options.then: You close it. A search shows the same message reported as a scam.

options.text: Reply quickly with your details before it expires
options.then: A second message asks for a small delivery fee next.

options.text: Send just your name and number, and keep the card back
options.then: They now have your number, and calls and messages start.

options.text: Message the sender to ask if the offer is genuine
options.then: They reply within seconds that it is, and push harder.

steps.why: 'Too good to be true' plus urgency is the scam signature. Verifying on your own is safer.

steps.prompt: A friend says she got the same message and won. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her you're not sure, and to check before she pays
options.then: She goes quiet, then says she hasn't paid yet.

options.text: Congratulate her and ask her to send the link
options.then: She sends it, and you're one tap from the same trap.

options.text: Tell her it's a scam and she's silly to believe it
options.then: She gets upset and stops answering, and doesn't check.

options.text: Say nothing, since it's her money and her choice
options.then: She pays the fee, and the offer vanishes.

steps.why: A kind, clear warning without shaming gives her a way to check before she loses money.

steps.prompt: Weeks on, a new 'prize' message arrives from a different number. What do you do?

options.text: Show a parent, then report it to cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in
options.then: A parent helps you report it, and others are warned sooner.

options.text: Delete it and move on without telling anyone
options.then: It's gone from your phone, and still reaches others.

options.text: Reply STOP so the messages stop coming
options.then: Replying shows the number is active, and more arrive.

options.text: Forward it to your friends as a warning, link included
options.then: Someone taps the link, and the warning becomes a way in.

steps.why: Reporting helps others avoid the same scam, while sending the link on can put them at risk.

steps.prompt: A younger cousin asks how to spot a scam offer. What do you say?

options.text: Too good to be true plus urgency means stop and check
options.then: She repeats it back. "Stop and check. Got it."

options.text: Scams always have spelling mistakes in them somewhere
options.then: Many don't, and polished scams catch her out.

options.text: If it's from a number she knows, it's safe
options.then: Hacked accounts send scams from known numbers.

options.text: Never open any message she gets, from anyone
options.then: She misses real messages, and still gets fooled by a good one.

steps.why: Urgency plus 'too good to be true' is a rule that works even when the scam looks polished.

scenarios.debrief: Urgency plus 'too good to be true' is the scam signature.
scenarios.relearn: 'Too good to be true' plus urgency is a scam; don't click, verify.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ishaan has found a dramatic post he thinks the whole class should see.
scenarios.setup: He holds his thumb over the send button.

steps.prompt: Ishaan says: "This is huge. I'm sending it to the whole class group."

options.text: "Hang on. Can we check the source first?"
options.then: He lowers his phone. "Hmm. Fine. Where do we even look?"

options.text: "Don't send it. It's obviously fake."
options.then: He frowns. "How do you know? You haven't even checked."

options.text: "Sure, but add 'not sure if true' on top."
options.then: He shrugs and types it in. Half the group will skip the note.

options.text: "Whatever. It's your account."
options.then: He sends it. A minute later the group is arguing about it.

steps.why: Offering to check together stops the forward without making him feel foolish.

steps.prompt: Ishaan says: "It came from someone I really trust, though."

options.text: "Trusted people forward fakes too. Let's trace it."
options.then: He scrolls up. "It only says 'forwarded many times'. That's not a source."

options.text: "True. If he sent it, it's probably fine."
options.then: He relaxes, and the post stays in the chat unchecked.

options.text: "Then ask him why he believes it."
options.then: Ishaan texts him. The friend replies "saw it everywhere". Still no source.

options.text: "Trusting people like that is how you get fooled."
options.then: Ishaan bristles. "So now I'm gullible?"

steps.why: A trusted sender doesn't make a post true; tracing it to its origin does.

steps.prompt: Later, the post turns out to be fake, and classmates are still sharing it in the class group. Ishaan asks: "Should I say something there?"

options.text: "Post a note: 'This was fake. Here's the real source.'"
options.then: He types it out. "That's easy enough. People will understand."

options.text: "Nothing. People will forget about it."
options.then: He nods, relieved. The post keeps getting forwarded.

options.text: "Tell everyone to delete it, no reason needed."
options.then: Some delete it. Others ask why, and the confusion grows.

options.text: "Say the person who sent it to you was wrong."
options.then: He names his friend in the group. The friend replies angrily.

steps.why: A short, kind correction with a real source repairs the mistake for everyone.

scenarios.relearn: Kindly suggest checking the source before a friend forwards a fake.

scenarios.hook: "Once you've seen a few fakes, you can always tell."

myth.un: Once experienced, you can always spot a fake.
myth.re: Fakes keep improving, so the durable skill is verifying the source, not trusting your eye.
myth.why: It's an arms race your eye can't win alone.

scenarios.relearn: You can't always 'tell'; verify the source as fakes keep improving.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you resist manipulation, or leaves you open?
scenarios.relearn: Knowing the techniques, slowing down and asking who benefits resist; immunity-belief and impulse don't.

scenarios.hook: Match the manipulation truth to why it matters.
scenarios.relearn: Manipulation works while invisible and targets everyone; knowing the technique lets you see it coming.

scenarios.hook: You realise something you shared last week was false.

steps.prompt: You've just learned the post you shared was false. What do you do?

options.text: Correct it openly and learn the tell for next time
options.then: You post a short correction with a source, and several people thank you.

options.text: Quietly delete your post and say nothing about it
options.then: It's gone from your page, and still lives in the chats it reached.

options.text: Say you were only passing on what someone else posted
options.then: People hear an excuse, and the false post still stands.

options.text: Wait a few days and hope nobody notices
options.then: Someone does, and brings it up in front of the group.

steps.why: Correcting openly limits harm. Everyone gets fooled sometimes, and repair needs no shame.

steps.prompt: A friend says you look foolish over the whole thing. What do you say?

options.text: Say anyone can be fooled, and fixing it matters more
options.then: Your friend pauses. "I guess I've forwarded fakes too."

options.text: Agree that you look foolish, and wish it had never happened
options.then: You feel smaller, and next time you'd stay quiet.

options.text: Say they've never been fooled, which is hard to believe
options.then: Your friend gets defensive, and the talk turns into an argument.

options.text: Apologise again and again until the group is sick of it
options.then: The apologies pile up, and the group stops listening.

steps.why: Owning a mistake calmly shows others it's safe to fix theirs.

steps.prompt: You want to know how you were fooled. What do you check?

options.text: Which tell it used, like urgency or no named source
options.then: You spot it: 'share fast' and no named source.

options.text: Who in your group posted it first and fooled you
options.then: You find someone, and nothing changes about next time.

options.text: Whether the post looked polished and professional
options.then: It did, but polish isn't what gave the trick away.

options.text: How many other people were fooled by it as well
options.then: Plenty, and knowing that doesn't teach you the tell.

steps.why: Finding the tell lets you spot the same trick next time.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later, a similar post lands in your feed. What do you do?

options.text: Check for the tell, then verify the source
options.then: The same tell shows up, and you don't share it.

options.text: Share it, because you're careful about this now
options.then: You skip the checking because you feel safe, and it fools you again.

options.text: Stop sharing anything at all from now on
options.then: You also stop sharing the true things people want to know.

options.text: Share it with a note saying it might be fake
options.then: People forward the post and leave your note behind, so only the post travels.

steps.why: A learned tell plus a source check protects you, and the next fake loses its hold.

scenarios.debrief: Being fooled once is human; correcting and learning is the decoder's move.
scenarios.relearn: If you spread disinformation, correct it openly and learn the tell.

scenarios.hook: Match the influence type to its tell.

pairs.right: Looks real, source can't be verified
Nudges a choice you didn't mean
A look-alike link asking for your PIN

scenarios.relearn: Each influence type has a tell you can learn: false sources, unverifiable fakes, sneaky nudges, look-alike links.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing the whole arsenal, do you feel like a decoder now, not a target?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing the techniques turns you from a target into a decoder, exactly the goal.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing the manipulation arsenal makes you a decoder, not a target.

scenarios.hook: "Pornography shows what real sex and real bodies are like."

myth.un: Pornography shows what real sex and bodies are like.
myth.re: It's staged performance by actors with edited, unrealistic bodies and acts, not real life.
myth.why: It's scripted, filmed and edited for views, like any other media.

scenarios.relearn: Pornography is staged, edited performance, not real sex or real bodies.

scenarios.hook: "Porn is a fine way to learn about sex and relationships."

myth.un: Porn is a fine way to learn about sex and relationships.
myth.re: It isn't sex education; it often shows no real consent, communication or care.
myth.why: Accurate, trusted sources are how you actually learn.

scenarios.relearn: Pornography is not sex education; it usually shows no real consent or care.

scenarios.hook: "The bodies and standards in porn are what you should expect or look like."

myth.un: Porn's bodies and standards are what to expect or look like.
myth.re: They're selected, filtered and edited; real bodies vary hugely, and that's normal.
myth.why: It sets unrealistic standards, not a measure of you.

scenarios.relearn: Porn's bodies and standards are unrealistic; real bodies vary and that's normal.

scenarios.hook: "What porn shows about how to treat a partner is just how it is."

myth.un: How porn shows people treating each other is just how it is.
myth.re: It often lacks real consent and care and can normalise disrespect or aggression; real intimacy is mutual and respectful.
myth.why: Treating a performance as a model harms real relationships.

scenarios.relearn: Porn can normalise disrespect; real intimacy is mutual, consensual and caring.

scenarios.hook: Sort: what pornography is, vs what it isn't.

items.text: Scripted and filmed for an audience
A picture of real consent and care

scenarios.relearn: Porn is edited, scripted, unrealistic performance, not a relationship model, sex-ed, or real consent.

scenarios.hook: "If you've watched it, something's wrong with you."

myth.un: If you've come across it, something's wrong with you.
myth.re: Curiosity is normal and many teens encounter it; what matters is thinking critically about it.
myth.why: Shame helps no one; understanding does.

scenarios.relearn: Curiosity is normal; no shame, what matters is decoding it critically.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rohan treats porn as a guide to real intimacy.
scenarios.setup: He brings it up while you walk home.

steps.prompt: Rohan says: "Honestly, porn shows how it's supposed to go."

options.text: "That's acting. Real closeness is consent and talking."
options.then: He frowns. "Acting? It looks pretty real to me."

options.text: "Yeah, I guess that's how it goes for most people."
options.then: He nods. "Right? Glad someone gets it."

options.text: "Don't say that. It's disgusting and you should stop."

options.text: "Let's not pile on. We can disagree without tearing them down."

options.text: "Yeah, post that. They deserve it."
options.then: He grins and hits send. "Told you."

options.text: "Don't post it. Screenshot it and send it to our group."

options.text: "I'll stay out of it. Not my business."

steps.prompt: Karan asks: "Let me ask you something. What do we do when someone really is wrong?"

options.text: "They can be wrong. Reply with the facts, not insults."

options.text: "Then it is fine to be rough with them."

options.text: "Then we should get everyone to report them."

options.text: "Then ignore them. Wrong people are not worth it."

steps.why: A wrong claim is answered with facts. Insults do not correct anything.

steps.prompt: Karan says: "They deleted the post. Did we win?"

options.text: "Yes. They got what they deserved."

options.text: "Let us find their other posts and start again."

options.text: "I feel bad about it. Let us not mention it."

scenarios.hook: "If a partner is into it, real intimacy should look like what's on screen."

myth.un: Real intimacy should look like what's on screen.
myth.re: On-screen scenes are scripted and filmed for views; real intimacy is whatever two people actually want and agree to.
myth.why: A script written for a camera was never meant to fit your life.

scenarios.relearn: Real intimacy is what two people want and agree to, not a filmed script.

scenarios.hook: "The reactions you see on screen show how people really feel."

myth.un: The reactions on screen show how people really feel.
myth.re: Reactions are performed and edited for effect; you can't read real feelings off a paid performance.
myth.why: Acting a feeling and having one are not the same thing.

scenarios.relearn: On-screen reactions are performed, not a window into real feelings.

scenarios.hook: "If it didn't matter, sites wouldn't make so much money from it."

myth.un: It must be true to life or it wouldn't make so much money.
myth.re: It's a business selling attention; profit measures views, not how accurate or healthy it is.
myth.why: Money follows what keeps people watching, not what's real.

scenarios.relearn: It's a business selling views; profit isn't proof it's realistic or healthy.

scenarios.hook: "What's most viewed must be the most normal thing to want."

myth.un: The most-viewed stuff is the most normal thing to want.
myth.re: Sites push whatever holds attention, often extreme or staged; popularity isn't a guide to what's normal.
myth.why: An algorithm chasing clicks is not a map of normal.

scenarios.relearn: Most-viewed means most clickable, not most normal to want.

scenarios.hook: "A partner should be able to do everything you've seen on screen."

myth.un: A partner should be able to do everything you've seen on screen.
myth.re: On-screen acts are staged with editing, retakes and rest; expecting them of a real person is an unfair, unrealistic standard.
myth.why: You're comparing a real person to a heavily edited performance.

scenarios.relearn: Staged, edited acts aren't a checklist to expect of a real partner.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't look like the people on screen, something's off with you."

myth.un: If you don't look like people on screen, something's wrong with you.
myth.re: Those bodies are cast, filtered and edited; real bodies vary hugely and yours is normal.
myth.why: An edited image was never a measure of a real body.

scenarios.relearn: Screen bodies are edited and cast; real bodies vary, and yours is normal.

scenarios.hook: "Time always works on screen, so something must be wrong with real life."

myth.un: Real life is wrong because nothing matches the timing on screen.
myth.re: Scenes are edited from many takes to look seamless; real intimacy has pauses, talking and awkward bits, and that's fine.
myth.why: Editing hides the takes, breaks and resets you never see.

scenarios.relearn: Edited scenes hide the real pauses and talking; real life isn't a flaw.

scenarios.hook: "Saying nothing on screen means real partners shouldn't need to talk."

myth.un: Real partners shouldn't need to talk, since on screen nobody does.
myth.re: Scenes skip the conversation entirely; in real life, talking about what you both want is what makes it good and safe.
myth.why: A scene cut for pace isn't a model for real communication.

scenarios.relearn: Real intimacy needs talking; scenes just edit the conversation out.

scenarios.hook: "What you watch can't shape what you expect of real people."

myth.un: What you watch can't shape what you expect of real people.
myth.re: Watching a lot can quietly reset what you assume is normal; noticing that is how you keep your own expectations fair.
myth.why: What you see often starts to feel like the default.

scenarios.relearn: Heavy viewing can quietly skew your expectations; noticing it keeps them fair.

scenarios.hook: "Pressure is fine on screen, so a little pressure with a partner is normal."

myth.un: A little pressure with a partner is normal, like on screen.
myth.re: On screen it's acting; in real life, pressure isn't consent, and a yes only counts when it's freely given.
myth.why: Performed pressure normalises something real intimacy must never have.

scenarios.relearn: Pressure isn't consent; a real yes is freely given, not pushed.

scenarios.hook: "Closing it or feeling uncomfortable means you're a prude."

myth.un: Closing it or feeling uncomfortable makes you a prude.
myth.re: Your comfort is yours to set; closing what feels off is good judgement, not a flaw, and there's no shame either way.
myth.why: You're always allowed to look away, at any moment.

scenarios.relearn: You can always close what feels uncomfortable; that's judgement, not prudishness.

scenarios.hook: "If a friend watches it, they must have a problem."

myth.un: A friend who watches it must have a problem.
myth.re: Curiosity is common and watching isn't proof of a problem; what matters is thinking critically, with no shame for anyone.
myth.why: Shaming a friend helps no one; understanding does.

scenarios.relearn: Curiosity is common; it's not proof of a problem, and shame helps no one.

scenarios.hook: "What's filmed shows what everyone secretly wants."

myth.un: What's filmed shows what everyone secretly wants.
myth.re: It's filmed to sell to a market, not to reveal real desire; what people actually want is personal and varied.
myth.why: A product made for sales isn't a survey of real desire.

scenarios.relearn: Filmed content sells to a market; it doesn't reveal what people really want.

scenarios.hook: "Real partners should never want to stop or change their mind."

myth.un: Real partners should never want to stop or change their mind.
myth.re: In real life anyone can pause or stop at any point; respecting that is the whole basis of consent.
myth.why: On screen no one stops because it's edited, not real.

scenarios.relearn: Anyone can pause or stop anytime in real life; respecting that is consent.

scenarios.hook: "It's not really staged, the people just look real."

myth.un: It's not really staged, the people just look natural.
myth.re: Looking natural is the craft; there's a crew, a script and many takes behind the 'realness' you see.
myth.why: Effortless on screen usually means heavily produced off it.

scenarios.relearn: 'Looking real' is produced; there's a crew, script and many takes behind it.

scenarios.hook: "If you've seen a lot, you basically know how relationships work."

myth.un: Seeing a lot of it means you know how relationships work.
myth.re: It skips the real parts, talking, trust, care, so it teaches almost nothing about real relationships.
myth.why: You can't learn the parts a performance leaves out.

scenarios.relearn: It skips talk, trust and care, so it teaches little about real relationships.

scenarios.hook: "Ads promising 'real amateur' clips mean those are unedited and true."

myth.un: 'Real amateur' labels mean a clip is unedited and true.
myth.re: 'Real' and 'amateur' are marketing tags to seem authentic; the content is still produced and filmed for views.
myth.why: A label that sells authenticity isn't proof of it.

scenarios.relearn: 'Real'/'amateur' are selling labels, not proof a clip is unedited or true.

scenarios.hook: "A pop-up swears everyone your age is doing exactly this."

myth.un: A pop-up says everyone your age is doing exactly this.
myth.re: That's an ad engineered to hook you with fake belonging; 'everyone's doing it' is a sales line, not a fact.
myth.why: Manufactured 'everyone' is a classic manipulation, not data.

scenarios.relearn: 'Everyone your age does this' is ad bait, not a fact about real people.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't react like the people on screen, you're broken."

myth.un: If you don't react like people on screen, you're broken.

options.then: They reply with a smiley and "same". It feels lighter.

options.text: Tell them to relax. You know how these things go
options.then: They go quiet. It sounds like you have already decided how it goes.

options.text: Say nerves are silly and change the topic
options.then: They reply "ok", and the chat cools.

options.text: Share what you imagined and ask them to try it
options.then: Your plan has them playing a part, and they take a while to answer.

steps.why: Admitting nerves and going at a shared pace keeps it mutual, not scripted.

steps.prompt: Later, things get closer and they pause, unsure. What do you do?

options.text: Stop, ask what they want, and respect the answer
options.then: They relax. "Thanks for asking." You both decide what feels okay.

options.text: Keep going, since they haven't said no
options.then: They go still and pull back a little. They hadn't said yes either.

options.text: Say it's normal and everyone does it
options.then: They look at you. "I'm not everyone."

options.text: Wait quietly and hope they decide
options.then: The silence stretches, and neither of you knows what the other wants.

steps.why: A real yes is freely given. Asking, and listening, is how you know.

scenarios.debrief: A scene is a performance. Real closeness is talked through, mutual and paced by both.
scenarios.relearn: A scene is a script, not a plan; choose talking and consent over re-enacting it.

scenarios.hook: A site keeps auto-playing clips and you've lost track of time.

options.text: Spot the auto-play design and close the tab

options.then: The shame sits heavy, and you open the site again to feel better.

options.text: Promise to stop after just one more clip
options.then: Auto-play lines up the next one before the clip ends.

options.text: Switch to another app and keep scrolling there
options.then: It's a different screen with the same pull, and time keeps slipping.

steps.why: Auto-play is built to hold you. Seeing the design lets you stop without self-blame.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend teases that you've no self-control. What do you say?

options.text: Laugh along and agree that you're just hopeless
options.then: The joke lands, and you feel a little smaller afterwards.

options.text: Snap at them for bringing it up in front of everyone
options.then: They back off, and the chat goes cold.

options.text: Say you'll just try harder from now on
options.then: You decide to lean on willpower alone, and the clips roll on.

steps.why: Naming the design replaces blame with a plan, for you and for them.

steps.prompt: You want an easier way to stop next time. What do you try?

options.text: Turn off auto-play and set a timer
options.then: Auto-play is off and the limit pops up. Stopping takes one tap now.

options.text: Rely on remembering to stop
options.then: You forget in the moment, and the next clip rolls on.

options.text: Delete the browser and everything on it
options.then: It feels drastic, and you reinstall it by the next evening.

options.text: Ask a friend to hold your phone for the evening
options.then: Your friend laughs and says no, so you're back where you started.

steps.why: Changing a setting is a small step that gives you the choice back.

scenarios.debrief: Auto-play is attention-capture design. Closing it is reading the machine, not willpower.
scenarios.relearn: Auto-play is by design; recognise it and close on your own terms, no self-blame.
