scenarios.prompt: Any of these is a good first question.
options: Who benefits if I share it?
scenarios.affirm: One question turns you from passing it on to actually decoding it.

scenarios.relearn: Reading the system, not just spotting lies, is the leap to digital wisdom.
scenarios.hook: Lensy: you've started reading the machine. What will you carry from it?
options: The feed is designed, so I can decode it
I can step outside my bubble
scenarios.affirm: That's the leap from media-literate to digitally wise, and it's yours to keep.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Sahil is about to forward a viral post to your group.
scenarios.setup: He shows you the number-one post at lunch.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "It's number one on trending, so it's obviously true."

options.text: "Trending means it spread fast. Let's check who sourced it."
options.then: He lowers the phone. "Spread fast? I thought that meant popular."

options.text: "Yeah, if it's trending this high it must be real."
options.then: He grins. "Exactly. Glad you get it."

options.text: "Maybe. Let's ask the rest of the group what they think."
options.then: He asks the group first. The replies are guesses, not checks.

options.text: "Who cares if it's true? It's fun to talk about."
options.then: He laughs and says everyone is already talking about it.

steps.why: Trending shows spread, not truth, so asking who sourced it is what matters.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "A friend just texted that it might be fake. How would anyone check a claim like this?"

options.text: "Find the first post, and see who made it and why."
options.then: He scrolls back. "Huh. The first post is from a shop page."

options.text: "Search the claim on a few other apps and compare."
options.then: He tries, and finds the same claim copied everywhere.

options.text: "Ask whoever shared it with you if it's real."
options.then: "They said it's real," he says. "They didn't check either."

options.text: "Look at how many likes and shares the post has."
options.then: "Loads," he says. "That's why it's number one."

steps.why: The first source shows who made the claim and why, which counts for more than any number.

steps.prompt: Sahil asks: "Okay, so should I share it or not?"

options.text: "Hold off until you've checked a source you can trust."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'll look first, then decide."

options.text: "Share it with a note saying you're not sure about it."
options.then: He adds the note, but others forward the post and leave it behind.

options.text: "Share it, but only to close friends and family."
options.then: He sends it to family, and it reaches the cousins by evening.

options.text: "Never share anything that's trending, ever again."
options.then: He frowns. "That seems extreme. Some of it is real."

steps.why: Holding off until the source is checked stops the claim at you.

scenarios.relearn: Trending measures spread, not truth; check the source before believing it.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin Ritika is about to forward a shocking 'leaked' clip to the family group.
scenarios.setup: She's already typing the message.

steps.prompt: Ritika says: "Everyone has to see this. I'm sending it right now."

options.text: "Wait. Let's see who posted it first."
options.then: She pauses, thumb over send. "Check what, exactly?"

options.text: "Go on, send it. They'll want to see it quickly."
options.then: She sends it. Within minutes, three aunts have forwarded it on.

options.text: "Send it, but add that you're not sure it's real."
options.then: She adds the note, and the clip travels without it.

options.text: "Don't send the clip. Just tell them what it shows."
options.then: She does, and the story spreads without any proof.

steps.why: A short pause to see the source stops a fake before it reaches the whole family.

steps.prompt: Ritika asks: "Some people are saying the clip might be fake. How do we check it?"

options.text: "See who posted first, and if a real outlet has it."
options.then: She searches. "The account is a week old. No outlet has it."

options.text: "Ask whoever sent it to you whether it's real."
options.then: "They said it's real," she says. "They didn't check either."

options.text: "Read the comments below it to see what people say."
options.then: "Half say fake and half say real," she says. "That doesn't help."

options.text: "Watch it again closely to see if it looks real."
options.then: "It looks completely real," she says. "That doesn't tell us much."

steps.why: Looks and comments can mislead. The poster and a real outlet are what you can check.

steps.prompt: Ritika says: "I'm still not sure about this clip. What do I tell the family group?"

options.text: "Tell them it's unverified, and say why."
options.then: She types it out, and two aunts reply with thanks.

options.text: "Quietly delete the message and say nothing."
options.then: She deletes it, and the clip stays on other phones.

options.text: "Message only the person who sent you the clip."
options.then: That person agrees, but the others never hear.

options.text: "Tell them all to stop using the family group."
options.then: Her mother frowns. "But we need that group for news."

steps.why: Telling the group openly, with the reason, helps everyone slow down next time.

steps.prompt: Ritika asks: "What do I do the next time something shocking comes?"

options.text: "Pause, find the source, then decide to share."
options.then: She nods. "Pause first. I can do that."

options.text: "Only forward things that come from family."
options.then: She nods, and a cousin's fake gets passed along the next week.

options.text: "Forward quickly and correct it later if it's wrong."
options.then: She tries it, and the correction never reaches everyone.

options.text: "Stop looking at anything that shocks you."
options.then: She frowns. "But some shocking things are real."

steps.why: Pause, source, then decide works on any forward, whoever sends it.

scenarios.relearn: Verify the source before forwarding; 'share fast' is engineered urgency.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Dhruv keeps saying you have no willpower for scrolling.
scenarios.setup: He says it again as you both look at your screens.

steps.prompt: Dhruv says: "You've got no willpower. You scroll for hours."

options.text: "It's built to be endless. Blame doesn't help."
options.then: He pauses. "Built to be endless? That's actually true."

options.text: "Yeah, I'm hopeless. I can never put it down."
options.then: He nods. "Yeah, you are. Same here."

options.text: "Look who's talking. You scroll even more than I do."
options.then: He laughs, and nothing about the scrolling changes.

options.text: "Whatever. I'd rather talk about something else now."
options.then: He shrugs, and the scrolling goes on in silence.

steps.why: Naming the design moves the blame from you to the feed, where it belongs.

steps.prompt: Dhruv asks: "But why can't you just stop when you want to?"

options.text: "Auto-play removes the stop, so I have to add one."
options.then: He nods slowly. "So the stop has to come from you."

options.text: "Because I'm weak. Some people are just like that."
options.then: He shifts. "I didn't mean it like that."

options.text: "I can stop any time. I just don't feel like it."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Sure."

options.text: "Honestly I don't know. It just happens to me."
options.then: "Same," he says, and neither of you looks up.

steps.why: Auto-play takes away the natural stopping point, so adding one is what helps.

steps.prompt: Dhruv asks: "Seriously though, what could we actually try?"

options.text: "Turn off auto-play and set a timer on both our phones."
options.then: He grins. "A timer. Fine. First to ignore it buys snacks."

options.text: "Just try much harder from tomorrow, both of us."
options.then: Tomorrow comes, and the old habits come with it.

options.text: "Delete every app and see how long we both last."
options.then: You both delete, then reinstall everything by the weekend.

options.text: "Compete over who scrolls less over the week."
options.then: It turns into a game, and you scroll more to check scores.

steps.why: Small design changes work better than willpower, and trying them together is easier.

scenarios.relearn: Long scrolls are by design; recognising the hook beats self-blame.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Meher says her view is right because her feed agrees.
scenarios.setup: She says it during a debate over lunch.

steps.prompt: Meher says: "Everyone I follow agrees with me. So I'm obviously right."

options.text: "That might be our bubble. Want to read the other side?"
options.then: She stops. "A bubble? I don't live in a bubble."

options.text: "True. If everyone I see thinks the same, it must be right."
options.then: She nods. "Exactly. Glad you see it too."

options.text: "Maybe. But I'd never read anything those people post."
options.then: She shrugs. "So we both stay put, then."

options.text: "You're right, and anyone who disagrees is just clueless."
options.then: She grins, and the debate turns into a pile-on.

steps.why: Agreement inside a bubble feels like proof, but it only shows what the feed lets in.

steps.prompt: Meher says: "Anyway, I follow hundreds of people. That's a lot of different views."

options.text: "Lots of accounts can still say the same thing."
options.then: She frowns. "Lots of accounts, one view. Hm."

options.text: "True. That many people can't all be wrong together."
options.then: She nods, pleased. "Right."

options.text: "Then your feed must be quite balanced, I suppose."
options.then: She smiles. "That's what I thought."

options.text: "Not sure. Let's drop it and go and eat lunch."
options.then: She shrugs, and the question stays at the table.

steps.why: Many accounts can repeat one view, so counting them isn't the same as comparing.

steps.prompt: Later, Meher asks: "If I wanted the other side, where would I even find it?"

options.text: "Look up a thoughtful account that argues it well."
options.then: She follows one. "Her points are actually careful."

options.text: "Search for people who disagree, and argue with them."
options.then: The argument heats up, and nobody changes their mind.

options.text: "Read the angriest post you can find from that side."
options.then: It's all insults, and it proves nothing to either of you.

options.text: "Nowhere. The other side isn't worth reading."
options.then: "Okay," she says, and the debate ends with nothing learned.

steps.why: A thoughtful account gives you the strongest version, so you can weigh it fairly.

scenarios.relearn: A like-minded feed is a bubble; you can't weigh views you're never shown.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Yash said 'just one thing' but is still scrolling.
scenarios.setup: You're waiting for him, and he hasn't looked up.

steps.prompt: Yash says, eyes on the screen: "Two more minutes. I'm just checking one thing."

options.text: "The feed never ends. Got what you came for?"
options.then: He looks up, startled. "Wait. How long has it been?"

options.text: "Same here. I always lose track of time when I scroll."
options.then: He laughs. "Ha. We'll both be here all night."

options.text: "Fine. Take your time. I'll just wait here for you."
options.then: He keeps scrolling, and another ten minutes disappear.

options.text: "Put it down right now or I'm going without you."
options.then: He snaps back. "Relax. I'm nearly done."

steps.why: Naming the design lets him notice the time without blame, so you both get going.

steps.prompt: Yash says: "I wasn't even enjoying it. Why do I keep going?"

options.text: "Scrolls are built so there's always one more post."
options.then: He frowns. "So it's the app, not me. Huh."

options.text: "Because you're weak. You need to try harder, man."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Maybe. Now I just feel bad."

options.text: "Because it's fun. Just enjoy it while you can."
options.then: He shrugs. "It stopped being fun ages ago."

options.text: "No idea. I wouldn't worry about it too much."
options.then: "Okay," he says, and the phone stays in his hand.

steps.why: Seeing the pull as design, not weakness, makes stopping feel possible.

steps.prompt: Yash asks: "What can I do so it doesn't happen again?"

options.text: "Decide what you want first, then close it when done."
options.then: He nods. "One thing, then done. I'll try it today."

options.text: "Delete everything and hide your phone for a week."
options.then: He tries, and by Sunday the apps are all back.

options.text: "Promise yourself you'll be stricter next time."
options.then: He promises, and next week it happens again.

options.text: "Keep scrolling until it feels finished, then stop."
options.then: It never feels finished, and he scrolls on.

steps.why: Naming a goal first gives him a natural stopping point, so he decides when to leave.

scenarios.relearn: Opening with intent and leaving when done is using the feed, not being used.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Anil shares an angry post in the class group chat.
scenarios.setup: Your phone starts buzzing with replies.

steps.prompt: Anil writes: "Just sharing this to see what people say."

options.text: "That post is built to make us argue. Let's not feed it."
options.then: Anil pauses. "I just thought it'd start a good chat."

options.text: "Ha, let's all go and pile on in the comments."
options.then: Dozens of replies later, the post is at the top of everyone's feed.

options.text: "Don't post stuff like that here. It's annoying."
options.then: Anil snaps. "Relax. It's just a post."

options.text: "I'm tapping the angry reaction, Anil. That'll show you."
options.then: The reaction counts toward the post, and nobody knows why you reacted.

steps.why: Outrage posts feed on reactions. Saying so, without a fight, stops the loop.

steps.prompt: Anil writes: "Anyway, so many people shared it. That means it's true, right?"

options.text: "Shares show spread. Who posted it, and from what source?"
options.then: He checks. "The poster has no source. Hm."

options.text: "Thousands of people can't all be wrong, so I guess."
options.then: He grins. "Exactly. So I'm right."

options.text: "Maybe. I haven't looked into it, to be honest."
options.then: He shrugs. "So we don't know. Still, it's a good read."

options.text: "Who cares whether it's true? It's wild to read."
options.then: He laughs, and the share count ticks up.

steps.why: Shares measure reach, not accuracy. The source tells you whether to believe it.

steps.prompt: A quieter classmate writes: "This post upset me. Can we stop?"

options.text: "Sorry it upset you. Let's take it down and move on."
options.then: Anil deletes it. The classmate writes, "Thanks. That helps."

options.text: "It's only a post. Please don't take it so seriously."
options.then: They go quiet and leave the chat.

options.text: "Then just mute the chat and the rest of us carry on."
options.then: They mute it, and the post stays up for everyone else.

options.text: "Let's vote on whether the post should stay up."
options.then: The vote drags on, and the post stays up all the while.

steps.why: Taking it down listens to the person who was upset, and removes the bait for everyone.

steps.prompt: Anil asks: "So what do I do when I see posts like that?"

options.text: "Ask who made it and why before you share it."
options.then: He nods. "Who made it and why. Okay. I can do that."

options.text: "Share only the ones that you strongly agree with."
options.then: He agrees, and those are the very posts built to spread.

options.text: "Share them with a warning that they're upsetting."
options.then: People forward the post and leave the warning behind, so it spreads without it.

options.text: "Skip anything that makes you feel angry at all."
options.then: He frowns. "But then I'd miss real news too."

steps.why: Asking who made it and why before sharing keeps you from feeding the machine.

scenarios.relearn: Outrage posts are engineered for engagement; sharing them feeds the machine.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Tanvi taps 'Allow all' on every app to get past permission screens.
scenarios.setup: She's setting up a new app beside you.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Allow all. I just want this screen gone."

options.text: "You can grant only what it needs. Let's look at each."
options.then: She hovers. "Wait. It's asking for my contacts. Why?"

options.text: "Same here. I always tap allow to make it go away."
options.then: She taps Allow, and the app now holds her contacts and location.

options.text: "It's fine. They've got all our data already anyway."
options.then: She taps Allow. "Right. Done."

options.text: "Better send the app's maker a message to ask."
options.then: She hesitates, then taps Allow anyway while waiting.

steps.why: Each permission is a choice, so looking at them one by one keeps your data yours.

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "Okay, but which permissions does an app actually need?"

options.text: "Match each to a feature. A camera app needs the camera."
options.then: She reads them. "It doesn't need my contacts at all."

options.text: "Whatever it asks for. The app knows best what it needs."
options.then: She leaves everything allowed, and the app keeps all of it.

options.text: "Contacts, location and photos, just to be safe."
options.then: She keeps all three on, and the app has her whole address book.

options.text: "Does it matter? They're all pretty much the same."
options.then: "Maybe," she says, and leaves it all on.

steps.why: Matching each permission to a feature shows which ones the app really needs.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "I've already allowed loads on my old apps."

options.text: "We can review them in settings and switch off extras."
options.then: She opens settings. "Wow. Some haven't been used in months."

options.text: "It's too late for that now. It's already out there."
options.then: She sighs, and the extra access stays on.

options.text: "Delete all those apps and accounts, every one of them."
options.then: She starts deleting, and loses a chat history she liked.

options.text: "Just use those apps a bit less from now on."
options.then: She uses them less, and they keep all the permissions.

steps.why: A settings review takes minutes, and it trims what old apps still hold.

scenarios.relearn: Grant only the permissions an app truly needs; your data and footprint last.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Isha believes an ad-style post because 'it knew exactly what I wanted'.
scenarios.setup: She shows you the post on her phone.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "It knew exactly what I wanted. It has to be true."

options.text: "It's targeting from your data. That doesn't make it true."
options.then: She blinks. "So it knows me because of my data? Hm."

options.text: "Spooky, how it gets you. It must be meant for you."
options.then: She nods. "Right? It's like it reads my mind."

options.text: "Check how many people have already bought it."
options.then: She finds happy reviews that all look the same.

options.text: "Ask the seller directly whether it's really true."
options.then: The seller says yes, of course it's true. It would.

steps.why: Targeting uses your data, so a post matching your wishes doesn't mean it's true.

steps.prompt: Isha says: "And it even mentioned the thing I searched yesterday."

options.text: "That's your search history at work. Check the seller."
options.then: She opens the seller's page. "No reviews. And it's brand new."

options.text: "Then it must be reliable. It clearly remembers you."
options.then: She nods happily, then hesitates over the payment screen.

options.text: "Clear your history and then the problem is solved."
options.then: She clears it, and the next ad finds her another way.

options.text: "Probably a lucky coincidence. Let's not overthink it."
options.then: She shrugs, and keeps the post open.

steps.why: A post that matches your history shows tracking, so check the seller instead.

steps.prompt: Isha asks: "So how do I tell if an ad is trustworthy?"

options.text: "Check the seller and reviews from outside the post."
options.then: She searches the seller's name. Nothing real comes up.

options.text: "If it feels like it was made for you, trust it."
options.then: She keeps it, and sees three more ads built from her data.

options.text: "Buy a small amount first, just to test it out."
options.then: She buys a little, and the seller asks for her card details again.

options.text: "Trust the ads that have a lot of likes on them."
options.then: The likes are from accounts that look new.

steps.why: Checking the seller outside the post tells you what the ad doesn't.

scenarios.relearn: Targeted content is built from your data; knowing you isn't proof it's true.

scenarios.hook: "It came on the family WhatsApp group, so it must be checked."

myth.un: If elders forwarded it, it's already verified.
myth.re: Forwards aren't checked by anyone; decode the content, not who sent it.
myth.why: A trusted relative can pass on a fake without knowing.

scenarios.relearn: A forward isn't verified just because family sent it; check the content itself.

scenarios.hook: "That voice note is clearly my favourite actor's real voice."

myth.un: A voice that sounds exactly right must be real.
myth.re: AI can clone a familiar voice now; verify the source, don't trust your ear.
myth.why: Sounding real stopped being proof, just like looking real did.

scenarios.relearn: A familiar-sounding voice can be AI-cloned; verify the source, not the sound.

scenarios.hook: "A screenshot of a chat is solid proof of what was said."

myth.un: A screenshot can't be faked.
myth.re: Screenshots are trivial to edit or stage; trace it to the real source first.
myth.why: A picture of text is not the text's origin.

scenarios.relearn: Screenshots are easy to fake; trace the claim to its real source before believing it.

scenarios.hook: "This account has a blue tick, so whatever it posts is true."

myth.un: A verified badge means the posts are accurate.
myth.re: A badge can be bought and only marks an account, never each claim.
myth.why: Verifying an account isn't verifying its facts.

scenarios.relearn: A blue tick marks an account, not the truth of each post; still check the claim.

scenarios.hook: "This dramatic clip is from the event everyone's talking about today."

myth.un: A clip going viral now must be from the current event.
myth.re: Old clips get relabelled as breaking news; check when and where it's really from.
myth.why: Recycled footage with a fresh caption is a classic tell.

scenarios.relearn: Viral clips are often old footage relabelled; check the real date and place.

scenarios.hook: "Thousands of people shared it, so it can't be made up."

myth.un: If huge numbers shared it, it must be real.
myth.re: Spread measures emotion and engagement, not accuracy; popularity isn't proof.
myth.why: Fakes go viral precisely because they're built to be shared.

scenarios.relearn: How much something is shared measures spread, not truth; popularity isn't proof.

scenarios.hook: "If the photo looks normal, there's no point checking it."

myth.un: A normal-looking photo needs no checking.
myth.re: A reverse-image search takes seconds and often reveals it's old or staged.
myth.why: The quick check beats the confident eye.

scenarios.relearn: A quick reverse-image search often exposes a recycled or staged photo in seconds.

scenarios.hook: "A warning this scary and urgent has to be passed on right away."

myth.un: Scary, urgent warnings should be forwarded fast.
myth.re: Manufactured fear plus 'forward now' is a manipulation tell; slow down and check.
myth.why: Urgency exists to stop you from thinking.

scenarios.relearn: Scary 'forward now' warnings use urgency to bypass thinking; slow down and verify.

scenarios.hook: "The message says I won cashback, so I enter my UPI PIN to receive it."

myth.un: You enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
myth.re: You never enter a PIN to get money in, only to pay out; that prompt is a scam.
myth.why: Receiving never needs your secret PIN.

scenarios.relearn: You enter a UPI PIN only to send money, never to receive it; that 'reward' is a scam.

scenarios.hook: "The caller sounds official, so sharing the OTP they ask for is fine."

myth.un: A convincing official caller can be given your OTP.
myth.re: No real bank or service ever asks for your OTP; the ask itself is the scam.
myth.why: The OTP is the last lock; only a thief needs it from you.

scenarios.relearn: No genuine service asks for your OTP; being asked at all is the scam signal.

scenarios.hook: "If a box is already ticked, the app must know what's best for me."

myth.un: A pre-ticked box is the helpful default.
myth.re: Pre-ticked boxes are a dark pattern set to benefit the app, not you; untick and read.
myth.why: The default is chosen for their gain, not your consent.

scenarios.relearn: A pre-ticked box is designed for the app's gain; untick it and read what you agreed to.

scenarios.hook: "I've heard this slogan so many times it must be true by now."

myth.un: Hearing something repeated often makes it true.
myth.re: Repetition only makes a claim familiar; familiarity isn't evidence.
myth.why: Endless repeating is a propaganda tool, not a fact-check.

scenarios.relearn: Repetition makes a claim feel familiar, not true; familiarity is not evidence.

scenarios.hook: "You can always catch an AI image by counting fingers in it."

myth.un: AI pictures always have obvious flaws like extra fingers.
myth.re: AI fixes its tells fast; the reliable move is checking the source, not hunting flaws.
myth.why: It's an arms race the eye alone keeps losing.

scenarios.relearn: AI fixes its visible flaws quickly; rely on verifying the source, not spotting glitches.

scenarios.hook: Sort each one: a manipulation tell, or a reliable signal?

items.text: "They don't want you to know this"
A link to the original report
All caps and ten fire emojis
A correction noted at the bottom

scenarios.relearn: Urgency, secrecy framing and caps are tells; datelines, source links and corrections are reliable.

scenarios.hook: Sort each message: scam signal, or a normal genuine one?

items.text: "Claim your prize, pay a small fee first"
Your order is out for delivery
"Your account is blocked, verify PIN now"
A bill reminder from your saved provider
An OTP you yourself just requested

scenarios.relearn: Pay-to-win, verify-your-PIN and pay-to-get-a-job are scams; expected updates and your own OTP aren't.

scenarios.hook: Sort each example into the influence family it belongs to.

items.text: A cloned video of a leader saying fake words
A fake countdown timer at checkout
An AI-altered photo of an event
A face-swapped clip passed as real

scenarios.relearn: Cloned and AI-altered media are deepfakes; fake timers, pre-ticks and false scarcity are dark patterns.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a step that verifies, or a reaction that spreads risk?

items.text: Forward to the whole family group
React before reading past the headline
Share because it made you angry

scenarios.relearn: Cross-checking, finding the origin and noting date and place verify; impulse forwarding spreads risk.

scenarios.hook: Sort each post by who it's really built to serve.

items.text: A how-to guide with no product push
Rage-bait engineered to get angry shares
A creator citing where they got their info

scenarios.relearn: Hard-sell urgency, rage-bait and chain dares serve the poster; sourced, honest help serves you.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a propaganda technique, or fair argument?

items.text: Painting one group as the enemy
Admitting a point against your side
Naming who made the claim and why

scenarios.relearn: Enemy framing, slogans and bandwagon are propaganda; checkable evidence and named sources are fair.

scenarios.hook: Sort each as a stronger or weaker source for a claim.

items.text: A primary document you can open

scenarios.relearn: Hearsay, anonymous forwards and linkless screenshots are weak; named originals and primary docs are strong.

scenarios.hook: Sort each interface move: dark pattern, or honest design?

items.text: A guilt button: 'No, I hate saving'
A plain price with no hidden add-ons
A countdown that resets on refresh

scenarios.relearn: Hidden exits, guilt buttons and fake timers are dark patterns; clear choices and easy cancel are honest.

scenarios.hook: Sort each habit: helps you resist influence, or leaves you exposed?

items.text: Assuming you're too clever to be fooled

scenarios.relearn: Pausing, asking who benefits and checking sources resist; shock-belief and overconfidence expose you.

scenarios.hook: Sort each profile clue: bot-farm tell, or a real account?

items.text: Made yesterday, posting 200 times a day
A stock photo as its only picture
A normal mix of likes and replies

scenarios.relearn: Brand-new, spammy, copy-paste, stock-photo profiles are bot tells; varied lived history reads real.

scenarios.hook: A fake clip is going around that puts a classmate's face on someone else.

steps.prompt: It lands on your phone from a friend. What do you do?

options.text: Don't share it, and let your classmate know
options.then: Your classmate is shaken, and grateful to hear it from you.

options.text: Screenshot it for a laugh with the group
options.then: The screenshot spreads, and your classmate pays for it, never knowing it started with you.

options.text: Ask the friend who sent it where it came from
options.then: They don't know, and it sits in two more chats.

options.text: Ignore it and hope it dies down on its own
options.then: It doesn't. It climbs, and more classmates see it.

steps.why: A fake of a real person is not a joke. Telling them, not sharing, protects them.

steps.prompt: Your classmate is upset and asks what to do. What do you say?

options.text: It's not your fault. A teacher or parent can help
options.then: They nod, tearful. "Okay. I'd rather not do this alone."

options.text: Tell them to ignore it until everyone forgets
options.then: They try, and the clip keeps travelling.

options.text: Tell them to find and confront whoever made it
options.then: They try to find out, and it turns into a fight.

options.text: Suggest they post a joke about it, to take the sting out
options.then: The joke makes the clip more visible, and the comments get cruel.

steps.why: Believing them, saying it isn't their fault, and bringing in an adult is the safest path.

steps.prompt: The class teacher says she has heard about a clip. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her what you know and offer to help
options.then: She thanks you, and says she'll look after your classmate.

options.text: Say nothing so you don't get dragged into it
options.then: The teacher has less to go on, and the clip keeps going.

options.text: Say it was only a prank that got out of hand
options.then: She takes it more lightly than the harm deserves.

options.text: Name whoever you suspect made it, without proof
options.then: Your guess may be wrong, and a classmate could be blamed unfairly.

steps.why: Telling a teacher what you know brings help fast, without guessing at blame.

steps.prompt: The clip is still on a few phones days later. What do you do?

options.text: Report it with your classmate and an adult: cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in
options.then: Your classmate agrees. An adult helps you file it, and the clip is reported for removal.

options.text: Delete your own copy and think that's the end of it
options.then: Your copy is gone, but the clip is still out there.

options.text: Message every person you can to delete their copies
options.then: Some agree, some laugh, and many never reply.

options.text: Assume someone else has already reported it
options.then: Nobody has. Everyone on the chat thinks the same, and the clip stays online.

steps.why: Reporting asks for its removal, with your classmate's say and an adult beside you. It is not their fault.

scenarios.debrief: With a fake of a real person, don't spread it; support them and report it.
scenarios.relearn: If a deepfake targets someone you know, don't forward it; tell them and report it.

scenarios.hook: A caller says your account will be frozen unless you read out the OTP now.

steps.prompt: The caller sounds urgent and official. What do you do?

options.text: Hang up, since no real service asks for an OTP
options.then: The line goes quiet, and your account is untouched.

options.text: Stay on the line and ask what happens if you refuse
options.then: They describe the freeze in detail, and the pressure builds.

options.text: Ask them to prove who they are before you decide
options.then: They quote a convincing employee ID, and keep pressing.

options.text: Ask them to call back later, after school
options.then: They refuse, say it must be now, and keep pressing.

steps.why: Pressure plus an OTP request is the scam. No genuine service asks for it.

steps.prompt: The caller rings back from a different number. What do you do?

options.text: Don't answer, tell a parent, and check the official app
options.then: A parent sits with you, and the app shows exactly what has happened to your account.

options.text: Answer and tell them firmly to stop calling
options.then: They stay on the line and keep pressing.

options.text: Answer and ask them to send an email instead
options.then: They email a link that looks just like the real bank page.

options.text: Block the number and don't check anything else
options.then: The account may be fine, but you never confirm it.

steps.why: Checking in the official app shows the truth. Blocking alone leaves you guessing.

steps.prompt: A friend says her father gave an OTP to a caller last week. What do you say?

options.text: It's not his fault. He should tell his bank and cybercrime 1930
options.then: She nods. "I'll tell him right away."

options.text: Say he should have known better than to read it out
options.then: She goes quiet, and he'll hide it longer.

options.text: Say it's too late now and nothing can be done
options.then: Waiting costs him more, and the money moves on.

options.text: Say he should keep it quiet and be more careful
options.then: Hiding it gives the thief time, and the shame grows.

steps.why: Acting fast and telling the bank and cybercrime 1930 gives the best chance, and it's never his fault.

steps.prompt: Your younger brother asks how to handle a call like that. What do you tell him?

options.text: Hang up, and check in the official app
options.then: He repeats it. "Hang up. Check the app. Got it."

options.text: Ask the caller lots of questions until they slip up
options.then: They're practised at answers, and he stays on the line.

options.text: Give the OTP only if they already know his name
options.then: Scammers often know names, so that proves nothing.

options.text: Stay calm and read the OTP out slowly, so it's clear
options.then: Calm or not, the OTP is still in their hands.

steps.why: No real service needs your OTP. Hang up and check the official app yourself.

scenarios.debrief: Pressure plus an OTP request is the scam; hang up and verify on the official app.
scenarios.relearn: A caller demanding your OTP under pressure is a scam; hang up and share nothing.

scenarios.hook: A message offers high-pay work from home if you pay a small registration fee.

steps.prompt: It says only a few places are left. What do you do?

options.text: Refuse, since real jobs don't charge you to join
options.then: You decline, and the messages stop for now.

options.text: Pay the small fee, since it's cheap next to the pay
options.then: After you pay, the number goes quiet and the 'job' vanishes.

options.text: Ask them to send proof of the company before paying
options.then: They send a glossy brochure, and keep asking for the fee.

options.text: Ask a friend to pay first and see what happens
options.then: Your friend loses the fee, and nobody gets any job.

steps.why: Charging to join is the mark of an advance-fee scam. Real work never asks for money upfront.

steps.prompt: A few days later, a new message offers the same job, with the fee split into two small payments. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, and check the company with a parent
options.then: A search you do together turns up reports from others who were fooled.

options.text: Agree to the instalments, since each seems small
options.then: The second payment is demanded, then a third.

options.text: Say you'll think about it for a week or so
options.then: They send daily reminders, each more urgent.

options.text: Ask your friends if they'd like to join with you
options.then: Two agree, and now you've all got money at stake.

steps.why: Splitting the fee makes it feel small, so a firm no and a company check beat any payment plan.

steps.prompt: A cousin says she paid the fee and is still waiting for work. What do you say?

options.text: Say it may be a scam, and report it at cybercrime 1930
options.then: She sighs. "I thought something felt off."

options.text: Tell her to wait a few more weeks, to be fair
options.then: She waits, and nothing arrives.

options.text: Tell her to pay for the next level to get started
options.then: She pays, and loses more.

options.text: Say it's her fault for paying in the first place
options.then: She stops talking about it and doesn't report it.

steps.why: Naming the scam, without blaming her, and reporting it helps her and others.

steps.prompt: The next time a 'job' message arrives, what do you check first?

options.text: Whether it asks for money, and who the company is
options.then: You check both, and the offer falls apart in a minute.

options.text: How high the pay is, compared to the work
options.then: High pay is the bait, so it pulls you in.

options.text: Whether the message looks polished and professional
options.then: Scams look polished, so this tells you very little.

options.text: Whether other people have already replied to it
options.then: Replies can be fake, or from people who haven't checked.

steps.why: Money upfront and an unknown company are quick checks that expose most job scams.

scenarios.debrief: Pay-to-get-a-job and urgency are the advance-fee scam signature; walk away.
scenarios.relearn: A job that charges you to join is a scam; genuine work never asks for a fee upfront.

scenarios.hook: A forward claims one home trick instantly cures a serious illness.

steps.prompt: It's from a relative's group and is spreading. What do you do?

options.text: Check trusted health sources before sharing
options.then: A health service page says there's no such instant cure.

options.text: Forward it because it might help someone out there
options.then: Someone tries it instead of seeing a doctor.

options.text: Try the trick yourself first to see if it works
options.then: It does nothing, and you've lost time you could have used well.

options.text: Ask the relative who sent it if she's really sure
options.then: She says she's sure, because three others sent it to her.

steps.why: A miracle cure can cause harm. Trusted health sources tell you what's actually known.

steps.prompt: Later, your relative tells you she sent that forward only because she wanted to help. What do you say?

options.text: Say you know she cares, and you'd like to check it together
options.then: She softens. "Okay. Let's look it up."

options.text: Say she should stop forwarding things to everyone
options.then: She feels told off, and stops talking to you about it.

options.text: Say nothing and let it go for the sake of peace
options.then: The forward keeps circulating in her group.

options.text: Say it's fine, because it can't really hurt anyone
options.then: Someone puts off a doctor's visit for it.

steps.why: Starting from her care, then checking together, keeps the relationship and the facts.

steps.prompt: A group member says they'll try it instead of seeing a doctor. What do you do?

options.text: Urge them to see a doctor before changing anything
options.then: They agree to ask the doctor first.

options.text: Tell them it's their choice and not your concern
options.then: They go ahead, and nobody has checked the risk.

options.text: Send them a long article about why it's false
options.then: They don't read it, and the plan stays the same.

options.text: Tell them to ask the group which cures worked best
options.then: Everyone offers a different story, with no evidence.

steps.why: A doctor can judge what's safe, so urging that visit is the helpful step.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how to tell if a health forward is trustworthy. What do you say?

options.text: Check whether a doctor or health service backs it
options.then: He saves the tip. "A doctor's source. Easy."

options.text: If lots of people have forwarded it, it's fine
options.then: Popular forwards can be the most wrong ones.

options.text: If it has a doctor's picture on it, it's reliable
options.then: Pictures can be copied onto any claim.

options.text: If it uses scientific-sounding words, it's probably right
options.then: Fancy words are easy to add to anything.

steps.why: A health service or doctor you can check is the quick test for any health forward.

scenarios.debrief: Miracle-cure forwards can endanger people; verify with trusted health sources first.
scenarios.relearn: Verify viral 'instant cure' claims with trusted health sources before sharing or trying them.

scenarios.hook: A shopping page flashes 'offer ends in 2:00' to rush you into buying now.

steps.prompt: The timer ticks down as you hold the item. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore the timer and decide calmly
options.then: You step away from the screen, and the pressure drops.

options.text: Rush to buy it before the timer reaches zero
options.then: You pay, and later notice the 'offer' is still on.

options.text: Add a couple more items to make the deal worth it
options.then: Your cart grows, and so does the total.

options.text: Take a screenshot of the timer and decide in a moment
options.then: The page resets the timer, and it shows 2:00 again.

steps.why: Fake countdowns create pressure. Deciding in your own time gives the choice back.

steps.prompt: Later, another item on the same site shows a timer and 'only 2 left in stock!' too. What do you do?

options.text: Treat it as more pressure, and check other sellers
options.then: The same item sits on another site with no countdown.

options.text: Believe it, since stock really does run out
options.then: You buy in a hurry, and the same notice is on every item.

options.text: Ask a friend to buy one before they run out too
options.then: Your friend panics, and you both buy something you hadn't planned.

options.text: Wait a minute and see whether the number changes
options.then: It drops to one left, then goes back up.

steps.why: 'Only a few left' is another pressure tactic. Comparing sellers breaks the spell.

steps.prompt: A pop-up offers an extra discount if you sign up in a minute. What do you do?

options.text: Close it, or read each box before you click
options.then: You find a pre-ticked box for newsletters and untick it.

options.text: Sign up quickly, so you don't lose the extra discount
options.then: You also agree to marketing messages you didn't see.

options.text: Tick everything so it goes through faster
options.then: A subscription is added to your order, and it's hard to spot.

options.text: Share it with friends so you all get the discount
options.then: They sign up too, and the pop-up spreads further.

steps.why: Pre-ticked boxes and pop-up urgency are designed to rush you. Reading takes seconds.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how to spot a fake timer. What do you say?

options.text: Refresh the page. If it resets, it's fake
options.then: He tries it. "It reset to two minutes. Wow."

options.text: If the timer is red and flashing, it's real
options.then: Red and flashing is exactly how these are made to look.

options.text: If a big brand uses it, it must be real
options.then: Big brands use them too, and size doesn't make it honest.

options.text: If it counts down very slowly, it's real
options.then: Speed isn't a test, because any timer can run at any pace.

steps.why: A timer that resets on refresh isn't tied to a real deadline.

scenarios.debrief: A countdown that pressures you is usually fake; decide on your own time.
scenarios.relearn: Checkout countdowns are often fake pressure; ignore the timer and decide calmly.

scenarios.hook: A dramatic 'breaking news' photo is spreading, but no outlet has it.

steps.prompt: Your friend wants to post it first. What do you do?

options.text: Run a reverse-image search first
options.then: It shows the photo is from an old event, years ago.

options.text: Share it as breaking news before others do
options.then: Your post goes up, and a comment says it's an old photo.

options.text: Zoom in to see whether anything looks edited
options.then: Nothing looks off, which tells you nothing about its source.

options.text: Ask the friend who sent it where it came from
options.then: He got it from a group, and that group got it from another.

steps.why: Being first with a fake spreads it. A reverse search shows where a photo came from.

steps.prompt: A friend says it doesn't matter, since the photo still feels true. What do you say?

options.text: Say a feeling isn't proof, so check where it's from
options.then: She thinks for a moment. "I hadn't looked at it that way."

options.text: Agree that the feeling is what matters most here
options.then: She nods, and the old photo keeps passing as new.

options.text: Say photos can't ever be trusted at all anymore
options.then: She shrugs, and the true photos get doubted too.

options.text: Say you'll let it slide this time, just once
options.then: It slides, and the next photo is shared the same way.

steps.why: A feeling isn't a source, so checking where the photo came from matters most.

steps.prompt: A real news outlet posts a similar photo with a caption. What do you do?

options.text: Compare the caption's details with the viral post
options.then: The caption names a different place and date.

options.text: Trust it fully, since it's from a news outlet
options.then: It's usually careful, but you didn't compare the details.

options.text: Ignore it and stay with the viral post anyway
options.then: You keep a claim the outlet doesn't support.

options.text: Message the outlet and ask why it differs
options.then: No reply comes soon, and the viral version spreads meanwhile.

steps.why: Comparing details with a credible source shows what holds up and what doesn't.

steps.prompt: Your group chat shares the photo again as new. What do you do?

options.text: Reply with the original source and date of the photo
options.then: People thank you, and several delete their posts.

options.text: Mute the chat so the photo stops bothering you
options.then: It's quiet, and the photo keeps spreading.

options.text: Say they're all fools for sharing it again
options.then: People get defensive, and the correction is ignored.

options.text: Reply 'it's fake' and leave it at that
options.then: Some doubt you, because you gave no source.

steps.why: A correction with a source and date is easy to check, so people believe it.

scenarios.debrief: If no real outlet carries a 'breaking' photo, reverse-search it before believing it.
scenarios.relearn: If no credible outlet has a 'breaking' image, reverse-search it before sharing.

scenarios.hook: A close friend just shared something you've checked and found is fake.

steps.prompt: It's already getting likes. What do you do?

options.text: Message them kindly with the real source
options.then: They reply with a thumbs up and say they'll check it.

options.text: Call them out in the comments, so everyone knows
options.then: They feel shamed, and get defensive in front of everyone.

options.text: Ignore it, since it isn't your business or your post
options.then: It collects more likes, and your friend hasn't heard a word from you.

options.text: Share their post with 'FAKE' written over it
options.then: It gets shared more, and the original still travels.

steps.why: A kind private message corrects the fake without shaming your friend.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend tells you they've seen the post everywhere, so it must be true. What do you say?

options.text: Say everywhere isn't proof, and share the source
options.then: They open the link, and read it twice.

options.text: Say it's fine, then, and leave it alone
options.then: The post stays, and so does the fake.

options.text: Insist you simply know better than they do
options.then: They dig in, and the chat goes cold.

options.text: Send them ten more links until they give in
options.then: They feel buried, and stop reading any of them.

steps.why: Spread isn't proof. One clear source is easier to read than a pile.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your friend admits they feel silly about the post. What do you say?

options.text: Say anyone can be fooled, and checking is the skill
options.then: They smile. "Okay. That helps."

options.text: Say they should have known better, honestly
options.then: They feel worse, and their replies get shorter.

options.text: Say that's what happens when you believe anything
options.then: They go quiet, and you've lost some trust.

options.text: Change the subject quickly, so it isn't awkward
options.then: The feeling stays with them, and the chat moves on awkwardly.

steps.why: Saying anyone can be fooled keeps trust, and makes checking feel normal.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend brings up the post that's still on their page. What do you say?

options.text: Say to add a correction with the source
options.then: They post a short correction, and two others do the same.

options.text: Say leave it, since everyone's moved on by now
options.then: It stays up, and keeps being shared.

options.text: Say delete it quietly and never mention it again
options.then: It vanishes from their page, but not from the chats it reached.

options.text: Say they should apologise to the whole class at once
options.then: It turns into a big deal, and they dread going in.

steps.why: A correction with the source repairs it better than deleting, and nobody needs to feel shame.

steps.prompt: A week later, a new fake appears in the group. What do you do?

options.text: Check it quickly, and message the sender kindly
options.then: Your friend joins you, and the message goes out with a source.

options.text: Leave it for the group admin to sort out
options.then: The admin is asleep, and the fake gets forwarded.

options.text: Post that it's fake without giving a source
options.then: People doubt you, and the argument starts over.

options.text: Mute the group until it all blows over
options.then: The fake stays, and you miss the group's real news.

steps.why: Quiet, kind corrections with a source become a habit your friends follow.

scenarios.debrief: Anyone can share a fake; correct a friend privately and kindly, decoding the content, not the person.
scenarios.relearn: Even a friend can share a fake; correct it kindly and privately, not by public shaming.

scenarios.hook: A fun quiz promises your 'true self' if you give it your number and contacts.

steps.prompt: Your friends have all posted their results. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it. A quiz doesn't need your contacts
options.then: Your friends tease you a little. Your number and contacts stay yours.

options.text: Enter a fake birthday but your real number
options.then: The result loads. The quiz still has your real number.

options.text: Fill it in. Everyone else did, so it's fine
options.then: Your result says 'creative dreamer'. Odd offers start reaching your phone.

options.text: Ask a friend who did it if it felt safe
options.then: She says nothing bad has happened yet. You still don't know what it collects.

steps.why: A quiz that asks for contacts wants data, not answers.

steps.prompt: A friend shares a second quiz from the same app and asks you to forward it. What do you do?

options.text: Don't forward it, and tell her what it collects
options.then: She checks the permissions list. "Huh. It does ask for a lot."

options.text: Forward it. People enjoy quizzes
options.then: Three classmates open it. Each one is asked for their number too.

options.text: Forward it with a note: 'don't give your number'
options.then: Some friends read the note and some just tap through, and the quiz collects from them.

options.text: Ignore the message and say nothing
options.then: The chain keeps moving without you. Nobody learns what the quiz asks for.

steps.why: Passing it on spreads the data grab; explaining it helps friends choose.

steps.prompt: Later, another quiz asks only for your location this time. What do you do?

options.text: Ask why it needs that, and close it if there's no reason
options.then: The page gives no reason, only a bigger 'Allow' button. You close it.

options.text: Allow it. Location is only one small thing
options.then: The quiz loads. It now knows where you are, and you never asked why.

options.text: Allow it for now and switch it off later
options.then: You forget to switch it off, and the app asks for your location every day.

options.text: Use a fake name and allow everything else
options.then: The quiz works fine. Your phone data still goes along with the fake name.

steps.why: Asking why an app needs data is the quick test: no reason, no permission.

scenarios.debrief: A 'fun quiz' demanding personal data is often data-harvesting; give it nothing.
scenarios.relearn: Quizzes asking for personal data are often harvesting it; skip them and keep info private.

scenarios.hook: A headline seems written to make you furious.

steps.prompt: Your blood is boiling and your thumb hovers over share. What do you do?

options.text: Read the full piece before doing anything
options.then: Halfway down, you notice the headline left out half the story.

options.text: Share it with a line saying how awful this is
options.then: Your post gets angry replies within minutes. Nobody mentions the article.

options.text: Send it only to one friend to vent
options.then: Your friend is furious too. Neither of you has opened the article.

options.text: Argue with it in the comments
options.then: The thread fills with anger, and your comment helps it reach more feeds.

steps.why: Reading the full piece first turns a reflex into a decision.

steps.prompt: Later, your feed serves another furious headline from the same site. What do you do?

options.text: Ask who gains from your anger
options.then: The site earns from every angry click. The headlines start to look alike.

options.text: Trust it this time. It might be real
options.then: It hits the same nerve, and the details are thin again.

options.text: Go by how many people shared it
options.then: The huge share count makes it feel solid. It only shows how many people reacted.

options.text: Ask the family group chat what they think
options.then: Two uncles are angry too and one says it's fake. The chat splits and nothing gets checked.

steps.why: Asking who benefits from your anger shows what a headline is built to do.

steps.prompt: A cousin forwards a furious headline and asks if you can believe it. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll read it first, and invite her to
options.then: She sends a thumbs-up. "Fair. I only read the headline."

options.text: Reply 'Unbelievable!' and forward it on
options.then: The headline reaches two more groups. By evening it's all anyone talks about.

options.text: Tell her she's gullible for sharing it
options.then: She goes quiet and doesn't open the article either.

options.text: Leave her message on read and move on
options.then: The message sits there. She forwards it to others who never read past the headline.

steps.why: A friendly 'let me read it first' slows a forward without shaming anyone.

scenarios.debrief: Outrage headlines are engineered to be shared on reflex; read fully and verify first.
scenarios.relearn: Rage-bait headlines are built to be shared on reflex; read the full piece and verify first.

scenarios.hook: You shared a post yesterday and have just found out it was false.

steps.prompt: Your post has already been reshared a lot. What do you do?

options.text: Post a correction and say what gave it away
options.then: A few people thank you. Others quietly delete their reshares.

options.text: Delete the post and say nothing about it
options.then: Your page is clean, but the reshares keep travelling without a correction.

options.text: Leave it up. A correction would be embarrassing
options.then: The post keeps travelling, and you feel a knot each time it gets a like.

options.text: Add 'maybe false' in the comments
options.then: Some people see it. Most don't, and the post still reads as true.

steps.why: An open correction reaches the people who saw the fake; deleting doesn't.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks whether you posted that thing, because it was fake. What do you do?

options.text: Own it and share what you learned
options.then: She laughs kindly. "It fooled me too. What was the tell?"

options.text: Say your account was hacked
options.then: She nods, but a mutual friend saw you post it. The story starts to wobble.

options.text: Blame the person who sent it to you
options.then: She asks who it was. The blame spreads, and the fake still circulates.

options.text: Joke it off and change the subject
options.then: She smiles. The fake stays in other chats, uncorrected.

steps.why: Owning a slip plainly turns it into something others can learn from.

steps.prompt: Next week, a post gives you the same jolt of shock as the fake did. What do you do?

options.text: Pause and trace the original source
options.then: You find a satire page behind it. This time, nothing goes out under your name.

options.text: Share it, since you can correct it later
options.then: You post it, then spend the evening checking replies.

options.text: Stop sharing anything ever again
options.then: Your feed goes quiet. Friends miss your posts, and you miss them.

options.text: Share it only with close friends
options.then: Your close friends pass it on to their own groups within the hour.

steps.why: Checking the source before you share is the habit that stops a repeat.

scenarios.debrief: Everyone gets fooled sometimes; the decoder move is to correct openly and learn the tell.
scenarios.relearn: If you spread something false, correct it openly and learn the tell, no shame, just repair.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two red flags in this 'bank' SMS.

scene.text: "Your KYC expires today, act now or account blocks"
It comes from a normal personal mobile number
Your bank's app shows no such alert
The official bank number is printed on your card
You can call the bank yourself to check

scenarios.why: Manufactured urgency and a personal-number 'bank' message are the scam tells; verify in the real app.
