steps.prompt: Someone says 'screenshot this for a meme' and tags you to do it. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it. You don't want your name on this later
options.then: You leave nothing of yours to be screenshotted back at you.

options.text: Join in. It's only a private joke
options.then: The screenshot leaves the group within a day, with your messages in it.

options.text: Take the screenshot but keep it only on your phone
options.then: A friend sees it on your screen and asks you to send it. Saying no gets harder.

options.text: Join in but use a nickname
options.then: Someone matches the nickname to you within a day. It was never hidden.

steps.why: A joke in a private chat can resurface with your name, so you can sit it out.

steps.prompt: The next day, the meme reaches school-wide chats and your class teacher looks upset. What do you do?

options.text: Don't share it, and tell her you're sorry it happened
options.then: She nods. "Thank you. It stung to see that."

options.text: Share it. It's already everywhere
options.then: More students see it, and the teacher's hurt grows.

options.text: Pretend you never saw it
options.then: The teacher notices who laughed. You feel uneasy all day.

options.text: Tell everyone who made it so they take the blame
options.then: People turn on each other, and the teacher still feels hurt.

steps.why: Not passing it on and saying sorry shows respect, even if you didn't make it.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says the meme is still going round, and asks the class what could help. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to report the posts and ask friends to delete theirs
options.then: She thanks you. Several classmates delete their copies, and the reports go in.

options.text: Say nothing. It was never your meme
options.then: Nobody offers anything. The meme keeps circulating.

options.text: Say it's pointless, since it's everywhere already
options.then: A few classmates nod and keep their copies. The meme stays on phones.

options.text: Post online to shame whoever started it
options.then: The post blows up, and a fight breaks out in the comments.

steps.why: Reporting and asking for copies to be deleted slows the spread, and an adult can help.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a friend jokes about roasting another teacher the same way. What do you do?

options.text: Say you're out, because posts can resurface
options.then: He rolls his eyes but drops it. Two others quietly agree.

options.text: Laugh and go along. It's different this time
options.then: The new chat takes off and the old story repeats.

options.text: Give him a long lecture about consequences
options.then: He stops listening halfway through and posts it anyway.

options.text: Say nothing but mute the chat
options.then: You mute it. The roast goes ahead without anyone pushing back.

steps.why: Saying you're out calmly, with a reason, can nudge others to think again.

scenarios.debrief: Your digital footprint lasts; a moment's post can outlive the moment.
scenarios.relearn: Post with future-you in mind; screenshots and footprints last.

scenarios.hook: A free quiz app wants your contacts, location and photos to 'work'.

steps.prompt: You really want to try the quiz your friends are posting. What do you do?

options.text: Deny what it doesn't need and use it anyway
options.then: The quiz still runs, and your contacts and photos stay private.

options.text: Tap 'allow all' so it stops asking
options.then: The quiz opens. It now has your contacts, location and photos.

options.text: Allow only location, since it feels harmless
options.then: The quiz still asks for the rest every time you open it.

options.text: Make a new email just for it and allow everything
options.then: The quiz works. Your phone's other details are still collected.

steps.why: A quiz doesn't need your contacts, so you grant only what it actually uses.

steps.prompt: A week later, another quiz app says it will 'stop working' unless you allow contacts. What do you do?

options.text: Uninstall it. A quiz can't need your contacts
options.then: The app disappears. Your friends' numbers stay with you.

options.text: Allow contacts. Everyone else did
options.then: The app messages a few of your friends with an invite from you.

options.text: Allow contacts for one session only
options.then: It uploads them in the first minute, before the session ends.

options.text: Read the reviews to see if others had trouble
options.then: Reviews mix praise with complaints. None explain what it does with contacts.

steps.why: If an app breaks without data it doesn't need, you can walk away.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if she should give a similar app her photos. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her to give only what it needs, and check
options.then: She taps through the settings. "It works without photos. Thanks."

options.text: Tell her to allow all for the full result
options.then: She allows everything, and the app keeps her photos on its servers.

options.text: Say an app wouldn't ask unless it needed it
options.then: She nods and allows it. The app only wanted the photos to learn more about her.

options.text: Tell her to skip every quiz forever
options.then: She sighs. "That's no fun. Everyone else is doing them."

steps.why: Apps can ask for more than they need, so grant only what the feature requires.

scenarios.debrief: Most apps work fine with the minimum; share only what's necessary.
scenarios.relearn: Guard your privacy: grant only the permissions an app truly needs.

scenarios.hook: Lately, bedtime has been the hardest part of your day.

steps.prompt: It's 11 pm and you've scrolled for an hour again, feeling worse. What do you do?

options.text: Swap the late scroll for a wind-down routine
options.then: You read a few pages and dim the lights. Sleep comes more easily.

options.text: Push through. You'll feel better eventually
options.then: The low feeling is still there when you wake up.

options.text: Scroll a bit more to end on something funny
options.then: The funny clip leads to five more, and it's midnight.

options.text: Switch to a different app that feels lighter
options.then: It feels lighter for ten minutes, then it's the same pull.

steps.why: Replacing the late scroll with a calm routine gives your mood a better chance.

steps.prompt: A week later, the low feeling is still there. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a trusted adult how the nights have been
options.then: Your aunt listens closely. "Thank you for telling me. Let's work out what helps."

options.text: Decide it's just you and nothing will help
options.then: The thought sits heavy. You stop trying anything new.

options.text: Wait another month to see
options.then: A month passes with the same heavy feeling.

options.text: Tell only a friend online and leave it there
options.then: She's kind, but she can't be there in person.

steps.why: Feeling low is never your fault, and a trusted adult can help beyond what a routine can.

steps.prompt: Your school counsellor puts up a notice about drop-in chats and Tele-MANAS 14416. What do you do?

options.text: Book a drop-in chat and save the number
options.then: The counsellor listens without judgement and shares a few simple next steps.

options.text: Think about it, then forget about it
options.then: The notice comes down at the end of the week, and the low feeling stays.

options.text: Wait until it gets much worse
options.then: A few weeks later, the nights are harder.

options.text: Ask online strangers if the counsellor is worth it
options.then: The replies are mixed, and none of them know you.

steps.why: A counsellor and Tele-MANAS 14416 are there to support you.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, a bad night comes round again. What do you do?

options.text: Use a calming routine and tell a trusted adult how it's been
options.then: The night is hard, but you're not alone with it, and it passes sooner.

options.text: Tell yourself it's just a bad night and ignore it
options.then: The night drags on, and nobody knows how it went.

options.text: Hide that it's happening again
options.then: You keep it inside, and the next bad night feels lonely.

options.text: Promise yourself you'll never scroll at night again
options.then: You break the promise by Thursday and feel like you failed.

steps.why: A calm routine and someone to turn to help on harder nights, and none of it is a weakness.

scenarios.debrief: If scrolling lowers your mood, change the habit and get help if it lasts.
scenarios.relearn: If a habit lowers your mood, adjust it and reach for support if it persists.

scenarios.hook: It's 1 am and you're tired, but afraid you'll miss something if you log off.

steps.prompt: Your eyes are heavy but the group chat is buzzing. What do you do?

options.text: Log off and sleep. The chat will still be there
options.then: You wake rested. The chat is full of in-jokes, and nothing that mattered.

options.text: Stay up so you're not left out
options.then: You catch the jokes, but you feel awful at school.

options.text: Stay up until the chat dies down
options.then: It never dies down. It's three in the morning.

options.text: Keep the phone under your pillow, just in case
options.then: Every buzz wakes you, and you doze all night.

steps.why: Fear of missing out is engineered, and sleep gives you back more than the chat does.

steps.prompt: In the morning, a friend asks if you caught the best part of the chat last night. What do you do?

options.text: Say how much you saw, and ask for her favourite bit
options.then: She tells you in two minutes. You laugh, and that's the end of it.

options.text: Feel annoyed and plan to stay up even later next time
options.then: The next night you stay up even later.

options.text: Scroll back through hours of chat to find it
options.then: You spend your morning reading and miss breakfast.

options.text: Pretend you saw every bit of it
options.then: She asks which bit you liked, and you struggle to answer.

steps.why: Asking takes a minute and keeps the friendship, so you miss very little.

steps.prompt: You want to take away the late-night pull. What do you do?

options.text: Set a night mode and charge it across the room
options.then: The buzz stops, and the pull feels lighter each night.

options.text: Rely on willpower to look away from the buzz
options.then: You hold out two nights, then slip.

options.text: Delete the group chat for good
options.then: Plans for the weekend start getting made without you.

options.text: Switch off notifications for everything, always
options.then: You miss a call from home and have to explain.

steps.why: A small change to the setup beats willpower, and it gives rest back.

scenarios.debrief: FOMO is manufactured; sleep and limits are a gain, not a miss.
scenarios.relearn: FOMO is engineered; choosing rest and limits is gaining, not missing out.

scenarios.hook: A video app seems to decide what you watch next.

steps.prompt: You only meant to watch one clip. The fourth is already playing. What do you do?

options.text: Turn off autoplay in the settings
options.then: The next clip ends and the screen waits for your choice.

options.text: Let it play. It's easier than deciding
options.then: Two more clips pass, and so does your evening.

options.text: Swipe to the next video, just once more
options.then: That one leads to another, and you're still watching.

options.text: Pause it and keep the app open
options.then: The app shows a 'continue watching' card with a trailer. You tap it.

steps.why: Turning off autoplay makes each video a real choice.

steps.prompt: A friend says autoplay is how she finds new things she likes. What do you do?

options.text: Say searching and choosing finds new things too
options.then: She tries it and picks two creators herself. "Huh. I like these more."

options.text: Agree and let autoplay run
options.then: The same loop returns, and your choices get quietly made for you.

options.text: Tell her autoplay is evil and she should quit apps
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "It's not that deep."

options.text: Say nothing and keep your own way of watching
options.then: She keeps scrolling, and you never talk about it.

steps.why: Autoplay isn't the only way to find good things, and choosing keeps it yours.

steps.prompt: The app now starts previews in a 'recommended for you' row. What do you do?

options.text: Find the setting that stops previews
options.then: You switch previews off. The home screen goes quiet.

options.text: Let it play. It's only a short preview
options.then: A preview turns into a ten-minute watch.

options.text: Uninstall the app for a month
options.then: The month passes. You miss the good parts of it too.

options.text: Look away and hope the sound doesn't catch you
options.then: The sound still pulls you back in.

steps.why: Hunting for the setting that stops it puts the choice back with you.

scenarios.debrief: Autoplay isn't an accident; switching it off reclaims your choice.
scenarios.relearn: Autoplay is capture design; turning it off makes each watch a real choice.

scenarios.hook: Your feed is full of fitness reels, and you've started comparing yourself.

steps.prompt: After an hour of fitness reels, you're frowning at the mirror. What do you do?

options.text: Unfollow the accounts that make you feel worse
options.then: Your feed stops feeding the comparison, and your mood lifts.

options.text: Keep watching to 'stay motivated'
options.then: You feel worse each time you look at yourself.

options.text: Follow even more fitness accounts to compare better
options.then: More edited bodies fill your feed, and the mirror gets harder.

options.text: Post a mirror photo to get likes and feel better
options.then: A few likes feel good for a moment, then you keep checking for more.

steps.why: A feed that makes you pick yourself apart isn't motivation, so curate who you follow.

steps.prompt: A friend shows you a reel and says she wants that body. What do you do?

options.text: Remind her reels are edited, lit and posed
options.then: She watches it again. "Right. The lighting is doing a lot."

options.text: Agree and ask which workout she'll copy
options.then: You both start a plan to look like that, and the comparison grows.

options.text: Tell her she's already fine, so stop
options.then: She feels brushed off and stops talking about it.

options.text: Tell her it's silly to care about looks
options.then: She feels dismissed, and the worry goes underground.

steps.why: Showing how reels are made helps her see that bodies vary hugely, and that's normal.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says exercise is only worth it if it changes how you look. What do you do?

options.text: Say it can be about energy and fun too
options.then: He thinks about it. "I do feel better after football."

options.text: Agree. Changing how you look is the point
options.then: You pick a plan based on how you want to look, and feel more pressure.

options.text: Tell him he's being shallow about it
options.then: He goes defensive. "It's not shallow. Everyone cares."

options.text: Change the subject and let it pass
options.then: The idea sits there unchallenged, and it keeps nagging at you.

steps.why: Movement can feel good for energy, sleep and fun without having to change how you look.

steps.prompt: Some days you still feel low about your body. What do you do?

options.text: Talk to a trusted adult or counsellor about it
options.then: Your sister says it's a common feeling and helps you find someone to talk to.

options.text: Keep it to yourself so no one thinks you're vain
options.then: The feeling stays, and nobody knows it's there.

options.text: Compare yourself with people in your class instead
options.then: The comparison shifts, but it doesn't ease.

options.text: Try an extreme routine you found online
options.then: It leaves you tired, and the worry doesn't shift.

steps.why: Feeling this way isn't vanity or weakness, and a trusted adult or counsellor can help.

scenarios.debrief: Curating your feed is a wellbeing habit, not vanity.
scenarios.relearn: Curate your feed: drop accounts that make you measure yourself harshly.

scenarios.hook: A photo you love has your school gate and uniform in the frame.

steps.prompt: You're about to post the photo and your friends are waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Crop out the school gate and name badge first
options.then: The photo still looks great, and nothing shows where to find you.

options.text: Post it as it is. Nobody's looking that closely
options.then: Someone you don't know replies with the name of your school.

options.text: Post it to close friends only
options.then: A friend screenshots it for her own page, and the gate is back in view.

options.text: Blur the background but tag the location
options.then: The blur hides the gate, but the tag points straight to the school.

steps.why: Small details add up to a map of you, so crop them out before posting.

steps.prompt: A friend tags your school in her own post that includes you. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to remove the tag and say why
options.then: She removes it. "I didn't think about that."

options.text: Leave it. It's her post
options.then: The tag stays, and others add theirs.

options.text: Untag yourself and say nothing
options.then: You vanish from the tag, but the school's name is still on her post.

options.text: Post an angry comment on her post
options.then: She feels called out in public, and the comments pile on.

steps.why: A quick, kind ask protects both of you and keeps the friendship.

steps.prompt: An app offers to add your live location to every post by default. What do you do?

options.text: Turn off location sharing for posts
options.then: New posts carry no location. You can still add one on purpose.

options.text: Leave it on so friends can find you
options.then: Each photo shows where you were, hours after you left.

options.text: Keep it on, since your account is private
options.then: Followers you barely know can still see each location.

options.text: Turn it off only on school days
options.then: Weekends and holidays still show where you are.

steps.why: Turning off automatic location means each post shows only what you choose.

steps.prompt: A new follower you don't know asks which school you go to. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it and tell a trusted adult
options.then: Your father helps you block the account. "I'm glad you showed me."

options.text: Say you'd rather not say and keep chatting
options.then: They keep asking, with a new question each time.

options.text: Tell them. They're probably a student
options.then: They don't reply. You never find out who they were.

options.text: Tell them and ask who they are first
options.then: They give a name that could be anyone's.

steps.why: Not sharing and telling a trusted adult keeps you safe, and none of it is your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Small details build a map of you; guard what your posts reveal.
scenarios.relearn: Guard your privacy: strip location clues before you post.

scenarios.hook: You keep losing time in apps you only opened for one thing.

steps.prompt: You open the app to message Isha, and the feed is right there. What do you do?

options.text: Send the message first, then decide if you're staying
options.then: You send it in a minute and close the app on your own terms.

options.text: Open the feed first 'for a second'
options.then: A second turns into twenty minutes, and you only send the message afterwards.

options.text: Send the message, then keep going while you're here
options.then: Twenty minutes later you wonder where the time went.

options.text: Set a five-minute timer, then scroll before messaging
options.then: The timer rings and you silence it, scrolling on for a while before you finally send it.

steps.why: Going in with a purpose lets you finish and leave on your own terms.

steps.prompt: Isha replies with a funny reel and tells you to watch it. What do you do?

options.text: Watch it, reply, then close the app
options.then: She sends laughing emojis. You're back to your work.

options.text: Watch it, then watch the five 'similar' ones
options.then: Five turns into fifteen, and you've forgotten your plan.

options.text: Tell her to stop sending you reels
options.then: She goes quiet, a little hurt.

options.text: Watch it later and leave the app open
options.then: The app stays open, and you drift back in within the hour.

steps.why: Doing what you came for, then closing the app, keeps the choice in your hands.

steps.prompt: You notice the same pattern every time you open a chat. What do you do?

options.text: Name your reason before you open an app
options.then: Opening an app now has a purpose, and you leave when it's done.

options.text: Tell yourself you'll be stricter next time
options.then: Next time looks exactly the same.

options.text: Delete the chat app altogether
options.then: You can't message Isha, and your plan to meet falls through.

options.text: Ask Isha to message you less often
options.then: She's hurt, and the habit is still yours.

steps.why: Naming your reason before opening an app turns an automatic tap into a choice.

scenarios.debrief: Going in with a purpose beats getting pulled into the loop.
scenarios.relearn: Open apps for a reason and leave when it's done; use tech on purpose.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rohan says late-night scrolling is wrecking his sleep and mood.

steps.prompt: Rohan looks worn out and says nothing helps. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest one phone-free night, and check in after
options.then: He agrees to try one night, and knows you'll ask how it went.

options.text: Tell him to just have more willpower
options.then: He shrugs. "I've tried that. It doesn't work."

options.text: Send him articles about screen time
options.then: He skims them and feels more guilty.

options.text: Tell him everybody's tired, so he'll be fine
options.then: He nods, but it feels like you didn't hear him.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Rohan says he still feels low most evenings. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's not his fault and suggest a trusted adult
options.then: He's quiet, then nods. "I think my mother would listen."

options.text: Promise to keep it secret and handle it together
options.then: He's relieved, but you can't help him on your own.

options.text: Tell him to snap out of it
options.then: He pulls back for a few days, then quietly comes back to you, still stuck.

options.text: Tell the whole class so people can help

steps.why: Taking his feelings seriously and bringing in a trusted adult is real support.

steps.prompt: Days later, Rohan says he may call Tele-MANAS 14416 and asks you to sit with him while he does. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes, and suggest his mother or a counsellor join too
options.then: He breathes out. "Okay. Let's ask her after school."

options.text: Say he should do it alone, since it's personal
options.then: He nods, but nerves stop him from calling.

options.text: Say yes, then do most of the talking for him
options.then: You speak for him, and he doesn't feel heard.

options.text: Say you'll think about it and get back to him
options.then: He waits for your answer, and the day slips by.

steps.why: Sitting with him while he calls, and bringing in a trusted adult, shows you're alongside him.

scenarios.debrief: Help a friend with a small step and real support, not shame.
scenarios.relearn: Support beats 'willpower': offer a step and a route to help like Tele-MANAS 14416.

scenarios.hook: Your post has fewer likes than a friend's, and you feel small over it.

steps.prompt: You keep refreshing to see the like count. What do you do?

options.text: Remind yourself likes track reach, not your worth
options.then: The number loses a little of its grip as you put the phone down.

options.text: Delete the post. Clearly it wasn't good enough
options.then: The post is gone, and the sinking feeling isn't.

options.text: Ask friends to like it so the count rises
options.then: A few likes come in, and the number still isn't what you wanted.

options.text: Compare your count with your friend's again
options.then: The gap seems bigger every time you check.

steps.why: Likes show how far a post was pushed, not how much you matter.

steps.prompt: A friend says timing and hashtags are why her post did well. What do you do?

options.text: Take it as a clue about reach, not about you
options.then: You see that reach depends on timing and tags, and your worth doesn't.

options.text: Copy her timing and tags to get more likes
options.then: Your post does a bit better, and now you chase the number.

options.text: Decide you're just bad at posting
options.then: You stop posting, and your friends miss it.

options.text: Say the algorithm is unfair and quit the app
options.then: You quit for a day, then drift back to the same feeling.

steps.why: Learning how reach works lets you see likes as distribution, not a score.

steps.prompt: A week later, a post you almost deleted gets many likes. What do you do?

options.text: Enjoy it, and don't read it as your worth
options.then: You smile, and the next post feels lighter.

options.text: Treat it as proof you're finally good
options.then: The next post gets fewer likes, and the sting is bigger.

options.text: Chase that style from now on
options.then: You post what you think will win, and it stops feeling like you.

options.text: Check the count every hour
options.then: The refreshing eats your afternoon.

steps.why: Likes rise and fall with timing, so they can't measure you either way.

scenarios.debrief: Like-counts reflect distribution and timing, not your worth.
scenarios.relearn: Likes measure reach, not your worth; don't hand a number the verdict.

scenarios.hook: You've decided screens are 'bad' and try to quit your phone cold turkey.

steps.prompt: It's day two without your phone and you feel cut off. What do you do?

options.text: Aim for balance: keep what helps, cut what drains
options.then: You keep messaging and study apps, and drop the late scroll.

options.text: Stay off completely and tough it out
options.then: You white-knuckle it for a week, then binge on the phone for hours.

options.text: Go back to everything exactly as before
options.then: Within days you're back at the same hours.

options.text: Ask a parent to lock the phone away until the holidays
options.then: You feel cut off from friends, and the plan strains things at home.

steps.why: Keeping what helps and cutting what drains lasts longer than all-or-nothing.

steps.prompt: A friend says the class study group has moved to a new WhatsApp group. What do you do?

options.text: Join it for the study notes and mute the rest
options.then: You get the notes and skip the memes.

options.text: Stay out of it and ask her to summarise
options.then: She forgets, and you scramble before the test.

options.text: Join every group, in case you miss something
options.then: The old chats pull you back in.

options.text: Say your phone rules are non-negotiable
options.then: The group moves on without you, and you feel left out.

steps.why: Using a tool for what it's good for is balance, not a ban.

steps.prompt: A video claims anyone who uses a phone daily is addicted. What do you do?

options.text: Question the claim and notice how you actually feel
options.then: Some of your use drains you and some doesn't. That's useful to know.

options.text: Believe it and feel guilty
options.then: You feel worse about yourself, and nothing changes.

options.text: Ignore it and use the phone however you like
options.then: You skip thinking about your habits, and the late scroll carries on.

options.text: Delete everything to prove it wrong
options.then: You regret it when your class starts a project chat.

steps.why: Noticing which uses help and which drain is more useful than a label.

steps.prompt: A month in, a parent asks how your phone use is going. What do you do?

options.text: Say what helps you, what drains you, and what you'll try next
options.then: She nods. "That sounds like a plan you made yourself."

options.text: Say you've quit screens completely
options.then: She looks at the phone in your hand, puzzled.

options.text: Say it's nothing and change the subject
options.then: The chat ends, and the conversation she could have joined never happens.

options.text: Say you just got tired of it
options.then: She nods slowly. You don't talk about what changed.

steps.why: Explaining what helps and what drains shows balance is your own plan, and it invites support.

scenarios.debrief: The aim is balance, not abstinence; the digital world holds real good.
scenarios.relearn: Aim for balance, not quitting: use the good, guard against the rest.

scenarios.hook: You have an old account from when you were 13 that you'd rather forget.

steps.prompt: You find it again, and the early posts are still public. What do you do?

options.text: Go through it and tidy or lock it
options.then: You delete a few posts and lock the rest. It now matches who you are.

options.text: Forget it exists. It's ancient history
options.then: A classmate finds it and shares a post in your class group.

options.text: Post a joke about the old you from that account
options.then: People dig deeper and find more.

options.text: Change your name on it and leave everything else
options.then: The posts are still public, and the old photos still show your face.

steps.why: You can still shape your footprint by curating what's public.

steps.prompt: A friend says she once found a cringey old post of yours. What do you do?

options.text: Laugh, then ask her not to share it
options.then: She grins. "Okay, deal. It stays with me."

options.text: Beg her to delete her screenshot
options.then: She shrugs. "Maybe I will." The screenshot is still on her phone.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Divya keeps saying everyone in her feed has a better life than her.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Meena has been unusually quiet lately.
scenarios.setup: She finally speaks up, watching how you'll react.

steps.prompt: Meena says quietly: "Honestly, I feel low most nights after scrolling."

options.text: "That's the design, not a flaw in you."

options.text: "Just stop scrolling then. Simple."
options.then: She nods, but her face closes. "Simple. Right."

options.text: "Everyone feels like that. Don't make it a big deal."
options.then: She nods and looks down. After a pause she speaks again.

options.text: "Maybe you're just too sensitive."
options.then: She flinches. "Maybe."

steps.why: Believing her, and saying it's the design and not a flaw in her, makes it safe to say more.

steps.prompt: Meena says: "I don't know what to do about it."

options.text: "Want to try a phone-free hour tonight?"
options.then: She tries a small smile. "Okay. One hour, and you'll check in on me?"

options.text: "Delete all your apps tonight."
options.then: She looks panicked. "But then I can't talk to anyone."

options.text: "I'll sort it out for you. Leave it with me."
options.then: She nods, relieved, but she hasn't tried anything herself.

options.text: "Sleep on it. It'll feel better in the morning."
options.then: She nods, and the next evening feels the same.

steps.why: A small, doable step with your company is easier to try than a big change.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Meena says: "The low feeling is still coming most nights."

options.text: "It's not your fault. Let's tell an adult."
options.then: She hesitates, then nods. "Maybe my mum. She noticed I was quiet."

options.text: "Give it one more week on your own first."
options.then: The week passes, and nothing eases.

options.text: "Let's keep it between us. Adults overreact."
options.then: She relaxes at first. The weight stays on you both.

options.text: "Ask the internet. There must be a fix somewhere."

options.text: "Then we try Tele-MANAS 14416, or someone else."

options.text: "Then drop it. It isn't worth the effort."
options.then: She nods tiredly, and the feeling stays.

options.text: "They will. Don't worry about it, honestly."
options.then: She looks reassured for a moment, but still unsure.

options.text: "Then handle it yourself. You're strong enough."
options.then: She bites her lip. "I wouldn't know how."

steps.why: If one person doesn't help, there are others, and Tele-MANAS 14416 is there for anyone.

steps.prompt: A month later, Meena says: "Some nights are better and some aren't."

options.text: "That's okay. Keep going, and keep talking."
options.then: She smiles. "Having you around helps."

options.text: "If you're not all better, you're not trying."
options.then: She sinks a little. "I am trying."

options.text: "Better nights mean you're fine. No need for more help."
options.then: She nods, but the rough nights get harder to bring up.

options.text: "Then forget the whole thing."
options.then: She nods. The old pattern returns on a rough night.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Aman's new app keeps asking for permissions he doesn't understand.
scenarios.setup: His thumb is hovering over the button.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "It keeps nagging me. I'll just allow it all."

options.text: "Hold on. It doesn't need your contacts."
options.then: He pauses. "Oh. So I can just allow what it uses? I never thought I could say no."

options.text: "Eh. Just allow it all so it stops nagging."
options.then: He taps allow. The app now has his contacts and location.

options.text: "Allow it, but check later what it took."
options.then: He forgets about it by dinner.

options.text: "Don't ever install apps like that."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Then I can't use half of what I need."

steps.why: A friendly flag before the tap helps him choose, instead of clicking through.

steps.prompt: A week later, Aman downloads another app that nags him. He asks: "What if it stops working unless I allow everything?"

options.text: "Try it with the basics. If it breaks, ask why."
options.then: He tries. The app works fine with only his photos allowed.

options.text: "Then allow it. It's their app."
options.then: He allows everything, and the app gets all of it.

options.text: "Then it's a bad app. Delete it."
options.then: He deletes it, though he wanted the editing tools.

options.text: "Allow it for now and switch things off later."
options.then: He forgets to switch anything off.

steps.why: Starting with the basics shows what the app truly needs.

steps.prompt: Aman asks: "How do I know what an app really needs?"

options.text: "Match each one to what the feature does."
options.then: He thinks. "So a map needs location, but a quiz doesn't."

options.text: "Ask the app. It will tell you."
options.then: The app gives a vague message, and the nagging goes on.

options.text: "Check how many people downloaded it."
options.then: A million downloads tell him nothing about what it takes.

options.text: "Just allow whatever it asks for first."
options.then: He allows the first three and wonders why it keeps asking for more.

steps.why: Matching each permission to a feature shows what an app really needs.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "My cousin's old apps probably have everything. Should I tell her?"

options.text: "Yes. Show her how to remove access."
options.then: Aman tells her. She checks, and removes a few permissions.

options.text: "No. It's her phone and her own call."
options.then: He nods. Her apps keep every permission they had.

options.text: "Tell her to delete every app she has."
options.then: She panics, then ignores him.

options.text: "Tell her it's probably too late now."
options.then: She feels hopeless, and does nothing.

steps.why: Showing someone where to remove access is kind and practical, and it's never too late.

scenarios.relearn: Flag a friend before they 'allow all'; grant only what an app actually uses.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Zoya has a screenshot from a private group chat that cracks her up.

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "This is so funny. I'm posting the screenshot."

options.text: "It has everyone's names. Let's keep it in the group."

options.text: "Go on, post it. It's funny and nobody will mind."
options.then: She posts it. By lunchtime, two classmates are upset with her.

options.text: "Post it, but blur the names out first."
options.then: She blurs the names, but everyone still recognises the chat.

options.text: "Send it to me first, then decide."

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "It's only a joke between a few friends. Does a screenshot really matter that much?"

options.text: "Screenshots travel. Anyone could pass it on."

options.text: "Right. Just a few friends. It's fine."

options.text: "Keep it for yourself and just don't show anyone."
options.then: She keeps it, and shows two friends 'just once'.

options.text: "Send it to the group so everyone's in on it."
options.then: The chat gets awkward, and one friend leaves the group.

options.text: "Share it, but only with a close-friends list."
options.then: The list includes people who know the others, and it spreads anyway.

steps.why: Deleting it ends the chance of it spreading, and the fun stays in the chat.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rishi is fed up with how much time he loses on his phone.

options.text: "It's just you. Other people manage it."
options.then: He looks hurt. "Wow. Thanks."

options.text: "Just set an alarm and stop when it rings."

options.text: "She's got a point. It's okay to ask for help."

options.text: "Don't. Adults overreact about phones."

options.text: "You don't need that. You're just bored."
options.then: He goes quiet, unsure whether to mention it again.

options.text: "Maybe later. First try the apps yourself."

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Rishi says: "I've cut it down to a few apps and it's actually going okay."

options.then: He frowns. "But it's actually going okay."

options.text: "Don't get too proud. You'll slip soon."

options.text: "Great. Now you're cured, so forget about it."

myth.why: Learning to read the machine, the message and yourself genuinely changes how you meet the world.

scenarios.hook: You've just moved to a new city and everything feels new.

steps.prompt: You're settling in and the groups keep multiplying. What do you carry with you?

options.text: The Decoder and your charter, and keep learning
options.then: You put your charter on your phone's home screen as a reminder.

options.text: Put the skills away now that the learning is done
options.then: In a few weeks, a convincing fake catches you off guard.

options.text: Trust everything your new friends share
options.then: A friend's forward turns out to be false, and so does the next.

options.text: Doubt everything so nothing can fool you
options.then: You tire of checking, and you start trusting nobody.

steps.why: The tricks evolve, so the Decoder stays useful for life.

steps.prompt: Your new roommate shares a striking photo of a 'real' news event. What do you do?

options.text: Check where it came from before reacting
options.then: A reverse search traces it to an AI art page. Your roommate laughs, a bit embarrassed.

options.text: Trust it. The details look real
options.then: It's convincing, so you pass it on.

options.text: Ask the group whether it looks real
options.then: Opinions split, and nobody can tell by looking.

options.text: Tell him it's definitely fake without checking
options.then: He asks how you know. You can't say.

steps.why: Looks aren't proof, so the habit is to check the source.

steps.prompt: An email says to click now or your scholarship form will lapse. What do you do?

options.text: Pause and check the official site
options.then: The site shows no such notice. You report the email.

options.text: Click fast so you don't lose it
options.then: The link opens a fake page asking for your details.

options.text: Reply asking if it's real
options.then: A reply arrives instantly, urging you to click.

options.text: Forward it to a friend to check
options.then: She clicks it, and you both feel uneasy.

steps.why: A pause and an official check take the power out of fake urgency.

steps.prompt: A friend says being critical online makes you cynical and boring. What do you do?

options.text: Say critical and kind can go together
options.then: He laughs. "Okay. So check it, be kind, have fun."

options.text: Agree and stop checking things so much
options.then: You stop checking, and the next fake fools you.

options.text: Tell him he's being naive about it
options.then: He rolls his eyes, and the chat cools.

options.text: Argue until he agrees
options.then: He stops replying, unconvinced.

steps.why: Critical and kind go together, and the real good online is worth keeping.

scenarios.debrief: What you carry forward, the Decoder and the charter, is the whole point.
scenarios.relearn: Carry the Decoder and your charter into adult life, and keep learning.

scenarios.hook: You want a digital-life charter you will actually keep.

steps.prompt: You sit down to write it. How do you start?

options.text: Write three short principles of your own
options.then: You jot: use it on purpose, check before sharing, be kind. It fits on one note.

options.text: Copy a long list of rules from a website
options.then: The list has twenty-five rules. By the next day you remember none of them.

options.text: Leave it blank and wing it
options.then: It feels relaxed. A week on, you scroll for an hour without deciding to.

options.text: Wait until you find the perfect wording
options.then: You keep meaning to finish it, and the first line never gets written.

steps.why: A few principles in your own words are easy to remember and to use.

steps.prompt: A week later, a shocking post lands in your feed. What do you do?

options.text: Check who made it before I share it
options.then: It comes from an account with no name. You hold off, and the post goes no further.

options.text: Share it fast and check after
options.then: Your friends react at once. Later you find out it was edited.

options.text: Check only if it looks fake to me
options.then: It looks real, so you pass it on. The look turns out to prove nothing.

options.text: Quit the app for good so nothing can fool me
options.then: The feed goes quiet, but so do your friends and the things you enjoy.

steps.why: Checking the source before sharing protects you and the people who trust you.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how you plan to keep your good online habits going. What do you say?

options.text: I will review my plan monthly and adjust
options.then: Your friend nods. "Maybe I should write mine too."

options.text: I will follow my plan perfectly, with no slips ever
options.then: Your friend smiles. One missed day, and you would want to drop the lot.

options.text: I probably will not stick to it, to be honest
options.then: Your friend shrugs. The plan stays a vague idea in your head.

options.text: I will remind everyone else to follow theirs
options.then: You start policing their phones, and your friend stops asking.

steps.why: A charter you can adjust lasts longer than one that demands perfection.

scenarios.debrief: A charter turns what you learned into how you'll live online.
scenarios.relearn: Write a digital-life charter: use it on purpose, check before sharing, be kind.

scenarios.hook: Your younger cousin just got their first phone and is already deep in the feed.

steps.prompt: They show you a video they cannot stop watching. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with them and show one decoding trick
options.then: You point out the autoplay. They laugh. "It never stops, does it?"

options.text: Take the phone away until they are older
options.then: They sulk, and the phone is back in their hands as soon as you leave.

options.text: Decide it is not your problem and scroll on
options.then: They keep watching. You feel a small twinge as you leave the room.

options.text: Explain everything wrong with feeds in one go
options.then: Their eyes glaze over. They nod, and keep scrolling when you finish.

steps.why: One small trick shared kindly lands better than rules or silence.

steps.prompt: Next week they ask why the same videos keep showing up. What do you say?

options.text: The feed shows what keeps you watching. Search something new
options.then: You search a new topic together. Their feed begins to change a little.

options.text: That is just what is popular. Everyone sees the same
options.then: They believe it. The idea that every feed is the same sticks.

options.text: You like them, so enjoy them
options.then: They shrug and keep watching, none the wiser about why.

options.text: Block all of them and be done with it
options.then: They block a few. New ones appear by evening, and they feel confused.

steps.why: Feeds pick what keeps you watching, and a new search shows you can steer it.

steps.prompt: Their friend sends a scary "forward to ten people" clip. What do you say?

options.text: Let us check the source first, then decide
options.then: You look together. Nobody official is named, and they hold off forwarding.

options.text: Forward it to ten people, just in case
options.then: The clip spreads through three groups before the evening ends.

options.text: Tell them it is definitely fake without checking
options.then: They believe you, but they still would not know how to check next time.

options.text: Say you will check it later and leave it
options.then: Later never comes. Meanwhile they forward it to a few friends.

steps.why: Checking the source together teaches the habit, which a flat verdict does not.

scenarios.debrief: Sharing the decoding habit is one of the kindest things you can do with it.
scenarios.relearn: You can pass the decoding habit on; sharing it spreads the skill.

scenarios.hook: After long scrolls you feel flat and down on yourself.

steps.prompt: It happens again tonight after an hour of scrolling. What do you do?

options.text: Put the phone down and do something offline
options.then: You walk to the balcony and call a cousin. The flat feeling eases a little.

options.text: Keep scrolling. It will pass
options.then: An hour later the flat feeling is still there, and it is much later.

options.text: Tell yourself you are being dramatic
options.then: You push the feeling down. It is still there when you wake up.

options.text: Check how everyone else is doing to see what is wrong with you
options.then: Every post shows a happier day than yours, and you feel worse.

steps.why: Stepping away breaks the loop. Feeds are built to keep you scrolling.

steps.prompt: You notice which accounts leave you feeling worst. What do you do?

options.text: Mute those accounts and follow ones that lift you
options.then: Your feed shifts over a few days, and scrolling feels lighter.

options.text: Keep them so you stay in the loop
options.then: You see everyone's best days, and the flat feeling comes back by the weekend.

options.text: Delete every app and go offline for good
options.then: There is relief for two days, then you miss your friends' news and your hobbies.

options.text: Study those accounts to see what they do differently
options.then: You spend hours on their posts, and your own days start to feel smaller.

steps.why: Curating the feed keeps the good parts of being online and drops what drags you down.

steps.prompt: Weeks later the low mood has not lifted. What do you do?

options.text: Tell a parent, teacher or school counsellor how you have been feeling
options.then: They listen without rushing and offer to find support with you.

options.text: Wait it out, since it will go away on its own
options.then: A few more weeks pass, and you feel more alone with it.

options.text: Tell only your online friends and no one else
options.then: They send kind messages, but nobody there can help you find support.

options.text: Decide it is just how you are now
options.then: You stop expecting it to change, and the low feeling has more room.

steps.why: If a low mood lasts, a trusted adult can help. It is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Tending your mental health is part of a healthy digital life.
scenarios.relearn: If scrolling lowers your mood, adjust use and reach for support if it persists.

scenarios.hook: A clip you reshared last week turns out to be a deepfake.

steps.prompt: You have just found out it is fake. What do you do first?

options.text: Post a correction and name the tell you missed
options.then: Your post gets a few replies. Someone writes, "Thanks for saying so."

options.text: Quietly delete it and hope nobody noticed
options.then: The clip is gone from your page. Three friends have already forwarded it.

options.text: Add a laughing emoji and say you were joking
options.then: A few people accept that. Others still think the clip is real.

options.text: Blame the person who sent it to you
options.then: They get defensive, and the argument is what everyone remembers.

steps.why: Correcting it openly repairs the harm. There is no shame in having missed it.

steps.prompt: A friend says they sent your clip to a big group. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them it is fake and ask them to tell the group
options.then: They post a note in the group. A few people say they are glad to know.

options.text: Tell them it is too late now. It is out there
options.then: The clip keeps circulating, and the group never hears otherwise.

options.text: Say sorry privately and leave the group alone
options.then: Your friend knows, but the group still thinks the clip is real.

options.text: Ask them to delete it without saying why
options.then: They delete it, puzzled. Others keep it, and nobody learns it was fake.

steps.why: Telling everyone who saw it stops the fake from travelling further.

steps.prompt: You want it not to happen again. What goes into your habit?

options.text: Check the source before I share anything shocking
options.then: Next time a wild clip arrives, you pause and look for where it came from.

options.text: Share only clips that look real to me
options.then: A sharper fake arrives and you cannot tell. The look proves nothing now.

options.text: Never share anything again
options.then: You stay quiet for a while, but miss sharing things that are true and good.

options.text: Share only after three friends share it first
options.then: Three friends share it, and none of them checked the source either.

steps.why: Checking the source works even when the fake looks perfect.

scenarios.debrief: Anyone can pass on a fake. What repairs it is saying so openly.
scenarios.relearn: If you spread something false, correct it openly and learn the tell.

scenarios.source: a friend who can't switch off
scenarios.hook: A friend says the feed runs their whole day and they cannot stop.

steps.prompt: They look worn out as they say it. What do you do?

options.text: Listen without judging and say it is not their fault
options.then: They let out a breath. "I thought it was just me being weak."

options.text: Tell them to use more willpower
options.then: They nod, but they look more ashamed than before.

options.text: Joke that you are hooked too and change the subject
options.then: They laugh a little, and the real worry stays unspoken.

options.text: Take their phone and hide it for the day
options.then: They are upset. The choice was taken from them, and the pull is still there.

steps.why: Listening first shows them the pull is by design, not a weakness.

steps.prompt: A few days later they ask what they should actually do. What do you suggest?

options.text: Mute extra notifications and set check times
options.then: They try it, and the day gets quieter. They still slip sometimes.

options.text: Delete everything and live offline
options.then: They last one day, and feel cut off from their friends.

options.text: Tell them to try harder from tomorrow onwards
options.then: They try harder, slip by noon, and feel worse.

options.text: Compete with me to see who can scroll less
options.then: It turns into scores and guilt, and it fades within a week.

steps.why: Small design changes like fewer pings make stopping easier than willpower alone.

steps.prompt: They say their sleep and mood have been poor for weeks. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest a trusted adult, and offer to go along
options.then: They agree. Having you there makes it easier to say.

options.text: Tell them it is just a phase and will pass
options.then: They go quiet, and stop mentioning how they feel.

options.text: Promise to keep it just between the two of you
options.then: They feel safe for now, but nobody who can help knows.

options.text: Work out what it sounds like and suggest a fix yourself
options.then: They start worrying about a label, and nobody who can help is involved.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help if it lasts. You stay with them, and it is not their fault.

scenarios.debrief: The pull is by design; warmth and support beat 'just try harder'.
scenarios.relearn: Stopping is design-awareness, not willpower; offer warmth and real support.

scenarios.hook: A brand-new app everyone is joining works in ways you have never seen.

steps.prompt: Your whole class is signing up tonight. How do you meet it?

options.text: Run the Decoder questions before diving in
options.then: You check who runs it and how it earns. It earns from ads, so it wants your time.

options.text: Assume my old skills will not apply and dive in
options.then: You tap around, and the app keeps pulling you to the next thing.

options.text: Skip it, since new apps are always a trap
options.then: You miss the class chat all evening, feel left out, and sign up the next day anyway.

options.text: Join because everyone has, and read the rules later
options.then: Sign-up takes a minute. You tap through the first pop-ups without reading them.

steps.why: The Decoder works on any new feed, so start with who made it and what it wants.

steps.prompt: A friend shows you its streak counter and badges. What do you make of them?

options.text: They are hooks, so I will use it on my terms
options.then: You turn off the badge alerts. Opening the app becomes your choice.

options.text: They are just fun rewards
options.then: You keep the streak for thirty days, and feel bad when it breaks.

options.text: I will keep the streak so I do not lose it
options.then: You open it at midnight to save the streak, and it eats into your sleep.

options.text: Everyone has them, so I will ignore it
options.then: You use it like everyone else and never wonder why it keeps pinging.

steps.why: Streaks and badges are attention-capture design. Naming them lets you choose.

steps.prompt: Later, the app asks for your contacts and location. What do you do?

options.text: Grant only what it needs and refuse the rest
options.then: It works fine without your contacts, and you can change it later.

options.text: Allow everything so the pop-ups stop
options.then: The pop-ups stop. The app keeps using both until you change it, and may copy your contacts.

options.text: Allow it for now and check settings later
options.then: Later never comes, and the app uses the permission every day.

options.text: Refuse every permission, even the ones it needs
options.then: The app cannot work, so you give up and tap allow on everything anyway.

steps.why: Granting only what is needed protects your data and keeps the app useful.

scenarios.debrief: Decode anything is one habit for life, even for the not-yet-invented.
scenarios.relearn: Decode anything: the habit applies to any new feed or app, for life.

scenarios.hook: You disagree with a stranger's post, and the comments are turning into a pile-on.

steps.prompt: Dozens of replies are mocking them. What do you do?

options.text: State your point calmly, about the idea and not the person
options.then: Your reply gets a few likes. The tone around it softens a little.

options.text: Join in, since they have it coming
options.then: You get quick likes, and the person stops posting.

options.text: Stay silent so nothing blows back on you
options.then: The pile-on grows, and you feel uneasy scrolling past.

options.text: Defend them loudly and attack the loudest critic
options.then: Now you are in the fight, and the argument becomes about you.

steps.why: You can question an idea clearly without tearing a person down.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend messages that the person deserved all of it. What do you say?

options.text: Disagreeing is fine. Cruelty does not make us right
options.then: They pause. "Fair. I got carried along with everyone."

options.text: You are right. They had it coming
options.then: They send a laughing face, and the thread feels even more justified.

options.text: I do not care. Let us talk about something else
options.then: They shrug, and the thread sits there unchanged.

options.text: Let us report them for being wrong
options.then: You report a post that broke no rule, and it stays up.

steps.why: Being right does not need cruelty, and saying so keeps you critical and kind.

steps.prompt: The next day the person posts again, sounding shaken. What do you do?

options.text: Be kind, and keep your one point calmly
options.then: They thank you for the tone and reply. The exchange stays civil.

options.text: Ignore it, since you have done enough
options.then: The post gets no replies, and the thread goes quiet.

options.text: Post another harsh reply to show you were right
options.then: The thread heats up again, and you leave feeling worse.

options.text: Agree with everything they say to be nice
options.then: It is polite, but you drop the point you actually believed.

steps.why: A kind tone with your point kept is what critical and kind looks like.

scenarios.debrief: Critical and kind, together: question the idea, don't crush the person.
scenarios.relearn: Be both critical and kind; disagree without tearing someone down.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Meera is piling onto someone in the comments and tagging you in.
scenarios.setup: A tag pings on your phone as she types.

steps.prompt: Meera messages: "Come on, tag-team this guy with me. He is so wrong."

options.text: "I will pass. We can disagree without tearing him down."
options.then: She sends a sulky emoji. "You are no fun."

options.text: "Yeah, go off. He deserves every bit of it."
options.then: She sends three laughing faces and posts a nastier reply.

options.text: "Okay, but I will only like your comments, not write any."
options.then: She is pleased, and your likes make her next reply bolder.

options.text: "Just stop tagging me. I am busy right now."
options.then: She stops tagging you, and carries on without a pause.

steps.why: You can disagree without joining a pile-on, and say so kindly.

steps.prompt: Meera asks: "Tell me something. What would you say to someone you think is wrong?"

options.text: "I would say what I think is wrong, politely, and why."
options.then: She tries a version. "Hm. That does sound less nasty."

options.text: "Nothing. Keeping silent is always the safest."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "So he just gets to say it?"

options.text: "Something clever that makes everyone laugh at him."
options.then: She grins, and drafts a joke at his expense.

options.text: "I would copy whatever everybody else is saying."
options.then: She nods. The thread gets another copy of the same insult.

steps.why: A polite reply that gives your reason keeps the focus on the idea.

steps.prompt: Meera says: "Others say I was harsh. Was I?"

options.text: "A bit. You can fix it with a kinder message."
options.then: She sighs. "Okay. I will write something fairer."

options.text: "No. He just cannot take a bit of heat."
options.then: She feels better for a moment. The thread stays as it is.

options.text: "Yes, you were awful. Everyone thinks so."
options.then: She goes quiet and defensive. "Thanks a lot."

options.text: "Forget it. It is only the internet."
options.then: She laughs it off, and still feels uneasy later.

steps.why: Naming it plainly and offering a way to repair keeps you honest and kind.

scenarios.relearn: Be both critical and kind online; both matter.

scenarios.hook: Your younger sister Anaya forwards you a shocking "breaking news" clip, thrilled.
scenarios.setup: Her message pings in a rush, just before dinner.

steps.prompt: Anaya texts: "Is this real?? Everyone is sharing it!"

options.text: "Cool find. Let us check the source before forwarding."
options.then: She sends a thumbs up. "Okay. I have never done that."

options.text: "If it is that dramatic, it is probably true. Send it on."
options.then: She forwards it to four groups. "Thanks!"

options.text: "It is fake. Delete it right now."
options.then: She deletes it, and still does not know what made it fake.

options.text: "I am busy right now. Ask one of your friends instead."
options.then: She sighs and asks her friend, who says it looks real.

steps.why: Checking the source together teaches her the habit, not just the answer.

steps.prompt: Anaya asks: "How do people actually check a clip like this?"

options.text: "Find who posted it first and check trusted news."
options.then: She searches. "Only random pages have it so far."

options.text: "Count the likes. More likes means more real."
options.then: She grins. "Twenty thousand! So it must be real."

options.text: "Does it look real? Then it probably is."
options.then: She watches again. "Looks real to me."

options.text: "Ask the group chat what everyone thinks."
options.then: Five people say it is real. None of them know who made it.

steps.why: Finding the first source and trusted news beats likes or how it looks.

steps.prompt: Anaya says: "New clip today, and I cannot find any source for it. Should I forward it anyway?"

options.text: "Hold off. With no source, we do not pass it on."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. I will tell my friends it is unconfirmed."

options.text: "Forward it, but add that you are not sure."
options.then: She does, and the clip still reaches fifty people.

options.text: "Forward it. Someone else will check it."
options.then: She sends it on, and so does everyone else who thinks the same.

options.text: "Delete it and never forward anything again."
options.then: She frowns. "Never? Even the real stuff?"

steps.why: With no source, do not pass it on, even with a note that you are unsure.

scenarios.relearn: Verify before you forward; teaching the habit passes it on.

scenarios.hook: You turned off most of your notifications this week.
scenarios.setup: At lunch, your friend Tara notices the quiet.

steps.prompt: Tara asks: "Why is your phone silent all of a sudden?"

options.text: "I want to use my phone on purpose, not be pinged around."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Huh. Does it work?"

options.text: "No real reason. I will probably turn them back on soon."
options.then: She nods. You feel the habit slipping before it started.

options.text: "Those apps were just annoying me. Never mind it."
options.then: She shrugs. The reason stays vague, even to you.

options.text: "I am better than people who check every single ping."
options.then: She stiffens. "Okay. That is a bit rude."

steps.why: Saying why you did it out loud makes your choice real.

steps.prompt: Tara says: "But what if you miss something important?"

options.text: "Calls and family still get through. The rest can wait."
options.then: She looks thoughtful. "That is fair."

options.text: "Then I miss it. That is simply the price I pay."
options.then: She winces. "Wow. That is a big price."

options.text: "You are right. I will turn them all back on tonight."
options.then: She smiles, and your phone starts buzzing again the same evening.

options.text: "Nothing online is important anyway."
options.then: She frowns. "My exam updates are online."

steps.why: Keeping calls and family on lets you cut the noise and stay reachable.

steps.prompt: Tara asks: "If I wanted to cut my own pings, how would I even start?"

options.text: "Pick the noisiest app and mute it for a week."
options.then: She tries it that night. "That was easy."

options.text: "Delete all your apps and see what happens."
options.then: She laughs. "I need those for school."

options.text: "Just copy exactly what I did."
options.then: She tries your setup, and it does not fit how she uses her phone.

options.text: "You would not manage it. You are too hooked."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Thanks for the vote of confidence."

steps.why: One small first step is easier to start than an overhaul, and it invites rather than judges.

scenarios.relearn: Use tech on purpose; saying why you chose it makes your choice real.

scenarios.hook: You decide to take a screen break tonight.
scenarios.setup: Your friend Dev watches you put your phone down and laughs.

steps.prompt: Dev laughs: "Logging off already? You are so boring."

options.text: "I am not quitting. I am choosing when to be on."
options.then: He tilts his head. "Choosing? Huh."

options.text: "You are right. I will stay on so I do not miss anything."
options.then: He grins, and you stay online long past when you meant to stop.

options.text: "At least I am not glued to my phone like you."
options.then: His smile drops. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "Ha. Yes, I am boring."
options.then: You pick the phone back up. He laughs, and you scroll again, feeling a little off.

steps.why: You can name a break as your choice without putting anyone else down.

steps.prompt: Dev says the next day: "Everyone stays on late for the good stuff. Are you coming?"

options.text: "Not every night. I want my sleep and focus back."
options.then: He shrugs. "Sleep, huh. I could use some."

options.text: "Then I will scroll till 2 am to keep up."
options.then: He laughs. You both stay up, and tomorrow is rough.

options.text: "If I skip it, I will be left out for good."
options.then: He nods. "People do remember who was not around." The worry stays with you.

options.text: "Nothing online matters anyway."
options.then: He frowns. "Some of it matters. Our class chat does."

steps.why: You can be honest about the trade and still choose time, focus and sleep over the fear of missing out.

steps.prompt: Dev asks: "So what is your plan? When are you on, and when are you off?"

options.text: "Balance. I pick the times and still go online."
options.then: He nods. "That actually sounds doable."

options.text: "I am going completely offline from now on."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "For good? That is a lot."

options.text: "Only when I start to feel guilty about being off."
options.then: He looks puzzled. "Guilty? Why guilty?"

options.text: "Only when I absolutely have to, honestly."
options.then: He grins. "So, basically never. Sure."

steps.why: Balance means choosing when to be on, not giving up screens.

scenarios.relearn: The aim is balance, not abstinence; a break is a choice, not a flaw.

scenarios.hook: You reshared a clip last week, and your friend Zoya has found something about it.
scenarios.setup: She holds up her phone with the debunk on screen.

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "Hey, the clip you shared last week was fake."

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. I will post a correction."
options.then: She smiles, relieved. "I was not sure how you would take it."

options.text: "Whatever. Everyone shares stuff. It is not a big deal."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "People believed it, though."

options.text: "Why did you not stop me before I posted it?"
options.then: She steps back. "I only just saw the debunk myself."

options.text: "I will just quietly delete it and move on."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Okay, but people have already seen it."

steps.why: Thanking her and correcting openly is repair without shame.

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "People are still sharing it. What should they hear about it?"

options.text: "That it was fake, how I checked, and what I missed."
options.then: She nods. "That helps people spot it too."

options.text: "Just that I am sorry to everyone."
options.then: She tilts her head. "Sorry for what? They will not know it was false."

options.text: "That it was a joke that went wrong."
options.then: She frowns. "But you shared it as if it was real."

options.text: "Nothing. A correction will draw more attention."
options.then: She sighs. "The fake spreads quietly, though."

steps.why: A good correction says it was false, how you checked, and what to look for.

steps.prompt: Zoya asks: "How will you catch the next one?"

options.text: "I will check the source before I share anything shocking."
options.then: She grins. "Can you show me how?"

options.text: "I will only share things that look real."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Fakes look real now."

options.text: "I will trust whatever my friends send me."
options.then: She laughs. "You trusted me. Do you check me too?"

options.text: "I will stop sharing anything online."
options.then: She looks surprised. "Even the true and good things?"

steps.why: The source check beats looks or trust, and it works on friends' posts too.

scenarios.relearn: If you spread something false, correct it openly and learn the tell; no shame, just repair.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Rohan has become very sceptical about everything he reads online.
scenarios.setup: He says it without looking up from his phone.

steps.prompt: Rohan says: "Everything online is a lie. Everyone is fake."

options.text: "We can question things without writing everyone off."
options.then: He pauses. "Hm. Not everyone, maybe."

options.text: "Yeah. Trust no one. It is all fake anyway."
options.then: He nods grimly. "Finally, someone gets it."

options.text: "That is silly. You are just being dramatic about it."
options.then: He crosses his arms. "I am being realistic."

options.text: "Then why are you online all day?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Habit. It is what everyone does."

steps.why: Questioning clearly while keeping the good is critical, not cynical.

steps.prompt: Rohan says: "But how do I know what to believe, then?"

options.text: "Check the source and who gains. Trust what holds."
options.then: He thinks. "That is more work. But it is something."

options.text: "Believe what you already agree with."
options.then: He grins. "That is easy. Too easy, maybe."

options.text: "Believe nothing at all. Then nothing can fool you."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Then nothing fools me. But nothing helps me either."

options.text: "Believe whatever has the most likes."
options.then: He laughs. "That is just everyone else's opinion."

steps.why: Checking sources and who gains is a real method. Believing nothing is not.

steps.prompt: Rohan says: "Okay, but is anything online actually good?"

options.text: "Plenty. Friends, learning, laughs. We choose on purpose."
options.then: He smiles a little. "Fine. The cricket clips are good."

options.text: "Not really. It is nearly all designed to hook us."
options.then: He nods. "Yeah. That is what I said."

options.text: "It is all fine. Stop worrying about it."
options.then: He frowns. "Some of it is not fine. Ads, scams, fakes."

options.text: "Some of it, but I would never trust any of it fully."
options.then: He shrugs. "So nothing really, in the end."

steps.why: The good online is real. Critical, not cynical, means questioning clearly while still seeing it.

scenarios.relearn: Be critical, not cynical: question clearly without giving up on the good.

scenarios.hook: Your younger friend Isha has watched you decode feeds all term.
scenarios.setup: She asks it quietly after your last class.

steps.prompt: Isha asks: "What will you do when something totally new comes along?"

options.text: "Ask who made it, what the trick is, and what is true."
options.then: She smiles. "That is simple enough to remember."

options.text: "Honestly, I will probably be lost, like everyone."
options.then: She looks worried. "Oh. I hoped you would know."

options.text: "Copy whatever my friends do and hope it works."
options.then: She nods. "That is what I do, too."

options.text: "Wait a year and see what happens to everyone else."
options.then: She laughs. "Then someone else tests it on you."

steps.why: The same few questions work on anything new.

steps.prompt: Isha asks: "What if the new thing is a better fake than anything before?"

options.text: "Then I verify the source instead of trusting my eyes."
options.then: She nods. "So the source matters more than the look."

options.text: "I will trust my eyes. I am good at spotting fakes."
options.then: She frowns. "Even experts get fooled."

options.text: "I will assume it is real if it looks real."
options.then: She hesitates. "Even a perfect-looking one?"

options.text: "Then I will avoid anything new altogether."
options.then: She looks sad. "But then you miss the good things too."

steps.why: As fakes get better, the source check is the defence that still works.

steps.prompt: Isha asks: "Will you ever stop learning this stuff?"

options.text: "No. It keeps changing, so it is a habit for life."
options.then: She grins. "A habit, not a lesson. I like that."

options.text: "Yes. I have pretty much learnt it all now."
options.then: She tilts her head. "But new things keep coming."

options.text: "Only when someone makes me do it."
options.then: She laughs. "So never, if no one asks."

options.text: "I will check in once a year or so."
options.then: She shrugs. "A year is a long time online."

steps.why: Decoding is a lifelong habit because the information world keeps changing.

scenarios.relearn: The Decoder applies to anything; you carry the questions for life.

scenarios.hook: A "free iPhone, claim now" link lands in your DMs.

steps.prompt: The message says the offer ends in ten minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Ask who benefits and check the source first
options.then: The sender is an unknown account. Nothing about it is official.

options.text: Tap the link before the offer expires
options.then: The page asks for your phone number and a small fee for delivery.

options.text: Reply to ask whether it is real
options.then: They answer within seconds, and push you to hurry.

options.text: Forward it to friends so they can claim too
options.then: Two friends tap it, and now the link is going round in your name.

steps.why: "Too good to be true" plus a countdown is the scam tell. Pause and check the source.

steps.prompt: Another message arrives with a timer and "only 3 left". What do you make of it?

options.text: Fake urgency, meant to stop me from thinking
options.then: You look closer, and the timer restarts each time you refresh.

options.text: Real urgency, so I should act now
options.then: You hurry. The "3 left" never changes, however long you wait.

options.text: Maybe it is real, so I will take a chance
options.then: You take the chance, and only your phone number goes out.

options.text: Test it on a friend's phone first
options.then: Your friend's phone opens the same page, asking for a number and a fee.

steps.why: Timers and low-stock numbers are pressure tricks. They are there to rush you.

steps.prompt: You suspect it is a scam. What do you do with the message?

options.text: Report it, block the sender, and tell a trusted adult
options.then: Your parent nods and shows you where to report scams.

options.text: Delete it and say nothing
options.then: The message is gone, but nothing is reported and no adult knows about it.

options.text: Keep it, in case it turns out to be real
options.then: It sits there. A week later another message comes from the same account.

options.text: Message them back to tell them off
options.then: They reply with a flood of new messages, and you feel worse.

steps.why: Reporting and telling a trusted adult helps others too. Being targeted is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: 'Who benefits?' and a source check defuse a scam before the urgency does its job.
scenarios.relearn: Run the Decoder on 'too good to be true + urgency'; ask who benefits.

options.text: I feel terrible, so I will stop posting anything

steps.why: Repair is the point. Feeling bad is normal, but fixing it comes next.

steps.prompt: You want to learn from it. What do you note about the post?

options.text: It had no source, and I did not check
options.then: Next time a post like that arrives, you look for the source before sharing.

options.text: That I should never trust anyone again
options.then: You stop believing even true posts, and feel cut off.

options.text: That it was just bad luck
options.then: Without a tell to remember, the next fake catches you the same way.

options.text: That I should only check exam posts
options.then: A fake about something else slips past, with no check at all.

steps.why: Naming the tell, a missing source, is how you decode better next time.

scenarios.debrief: Decoding includes the repair: correct it openly and learn the tell.
scenarios.relearn: If you spread something false, correct it openly and learn the tell, no shame.

scenarios.hook: A checkout page has a pre-ticked "add insurance ₹299" box.

steps.prompt: You are buying earphones and about to tap Pay. What do you do?

options.text: Spot the pre-ticked box and untick it
options.then: The total drops by ₹299. You never asked for the insurance.

options.text: Leave it ticked, since it was already on
options.then: The total stays ₹299 higher than you planned, and you scroll on to the next screen.

options.text: Leave it, since it is only ₹299
options.then: It is a small amount, and you never ask whether you needed it.

options.text: Ask the seller's chat if I need it
options.then: The reply says "highly recommended", and the box stays ticked.

steps.prompt: A countdown shows the price rising in two minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore the clock and check the price elsewhere
options.then: The same earphones are available at that price for days.

options.text: Rush to the last step before it ends
options.then: You rush, and skim past the extras added at the last step.

options.text: Decide fast and compare prices later, if I remember
options.then: You hurry on, and the last step loads before you have compared anything.

options.text: Trust it, since countdowns are always accurate
options.then: The clock restarts when you refresh. It was never real.

steps.why: A fake countdown is built to rush you. Pausing takes the pressure away.

steps.prompt: At the last step, "Cancel" is tiny and "Yes, add it" is huge. What do you do?

options.text: Notice the trick and choose what I want
options.then: You find the small button and keep only what you chose.

options.text: Tap the big button, since it must be right
options.then: The extra gets added, and you only notice on the receipt.

options.text: Give up and pay anyway
options.then: You pay for things you did not want, feeling tricked.

options.text: Tell all my friends never to shop online
