scenarios.debrief: The Decoder names the technique, a pre-ticked box, and undoes it.
scenarios.relearn: Spot dark patterns like pre-ticked boxes; choose on purpose.

scenarios.hook: A screenshot "quote" from a leader is spreading fast.

steps.prompt: It looks like a screenshot of their post, and everyone is angry. What do you do?

options.text: Search whether they actually said it
options.then: You find no such post on their real account. The screenshot has no link.

options.text: React because everyone else already has
options.then: You join the anger, and the quote is false.

options.text: Share it with a note asking if it is real
options.then: People see the screenshot, and few read your note.

options.text: Trust it, since it has their photo and name
options.then: You pass it on. Later someone shows the photo and name were copied from the real account.

steps.why: A screenshot is easy to fake. Verify the quote at its source first.

steps.prompt: A friend says: "Screenshots cannot be faked." What do you say?

options.text: They are easy to fake. Let us check the original post
options.then: You look together. The original does not exist.

options.text: You are right, so it must be true
options.then: You both believe it, and it spreads further.

options.text: Maybe, but this one looks too perfect to be fake
options.then: You both stay with how it looks, and your friend forwards it as proof.

options.text: Nothing. Arguing is pointless
options.then: The belief stays, and your friend forwards it.

steps.prompt: The leader's real account has nothing like it. What do you do?

options.text: Tell those who shared it, and show what I found
options.then: Some delete it. One writes back: "I wish I had checked before."

options.text: Delete my copy and say nothing
options.then: Your copy is gone, but others keep sharing it.

options.text: Say they deleted it to hide it
options.then: That is a guess, and it spreads as if it were a fact.

options.text: Keep sharing it, since it sounds like them
options.then: The quote travels further, with nothing real behind it.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder verifies a quote at the source before letting it move you.
scenarios.relearn: Verify a viral quote at its source before reacting or sharing.

scenarios.hook: You have five seconds, and a claim feels true.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you to confirm it before the bus leaves. What do you do?

options.text: Use the five seconds to check the source
options.then: You find it quickly. It is a joke page.

options.text: Go with the feeling, since we are in a hurry
options.then: You say yes, and your friend repeats it to the whole bus.

options.text: Say it is true because most people agree
options.then: Most people agree because they saw the same post.

options.text: Say I will check it when I get home
options.then: Hours later, the claim has been repeated in three chats.

steps.why: Even five seconds on the source turns a gut feeling into a checked one.

steps.prompt: The claim comes with a photo as proof. What do you do?

options.text: Ask where the photo comes from
options.then: A quick search shows it is from a different event.

options.text: Take the photo as proof
options.then: The photo is real, but it belongs to something else.

options.text: Zoom in for details that look real
options.then: The details look convincing, and say nothing about where it was taken.

options.text: Ask if anyone else believes it
options.then: Several do, and none can say where the photo came from.

steps.why: A photo shows an image, not the story attached to it. Check where it is from.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks whether to share it. What do you say?

options.text: Hold off unless a real source backs it
options.then: Your friend nods and pockets the phone. "Okay. Not without a source."

options.text: Share it, since it feels right
options.then: Your friend shares it, and a classmate asks for proof you do not have.

options.text: Share it, then check on the bus
options.then: The check finds it false, after fifty people have seen it.

options.text: Never share anything, to be safe
options.then: Your friend rolls their eyes. "Even real news?"

steps.why: Hold off unless a trusted source backs it. A true claim will still be true in a minute.

scenarios.debrief: Even a few seconds of pause turns a gut reaction into a decoded one.
scenarios.relearn: Build in a short pause; decoding beats reacting in a hurry.

scenarios.hook: A "survey" offers a prize if you enter your bank OTP.

steps.prompt: The survey asks for the OTP just sent to you. What do you do?

options.text: Stop. No real prize needs my OTP
options.then: You close the page. The OTP stays with you, and the page keeps pinging.

options.text: Enter it quickly so I do not miss the prize
options.then: The page says "processing", and your bank sends an alert. You tell a parent right away.

options.text: Enter it, since the survey page looks official
options.then: Nothing happens for a day. Then your bank texts about a payment you did not make.

options.text: Ask friends if they got the prize too
options.then: Two say they got the same text, and no one knows what is real.

steps.why: An OTP request is the scam tell. A genuine prize never needs it.

steps.prompt: A friend says she already entered hers and has heard nothing. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to contact her bank and a trusted adult
options.then: She calls the bank. They tell her what to do next.

options.text: Tell her not to worry. It will come
options.then: She waits for days, and nothing arrives.

options.text: Tell her it is her own fault for entering it
options.then: She stops talking, and feels more alone with it.

options.text: Tell her to enter it again to be sure
options.then: The page asks for more details, and the situation gets worse.

steps.why: It is not her fault. A scam is built to fool people, so help her act quickly.

steps.prompt: You want to report the survey. Where do you go?

options.text: Report it on cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in
options.then: The report goes in, and you tell your parent as well.

options.text: Block the number and move on
options.then: The number is blocked, but the scam goes on for others.

options.text: Post a warning only in my story
options.then: Some friends see it, but nobody reports the scam itself.

options.text: Reply to the sender to say I know it is a scam
options.then: They stop replying, and move on to someone else.

steps.why: Reporting via cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in helps stop it for others too.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder spots the OTP-bait scam and uses the real report route.
scenarios.relearn: No genuine prize needs your OTP; report scams: cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in.

scenarios.hook: A claim flatters exactly what you already believe.

steps.prompt: A post agrees with everything you think. What do you do?

options.text: Decode it harder, because I agree with it
options.then: You look for the source. The post leaves out one fact that does not fit.

options.text: Share it, since it matches what I think
options.then: Your friends agree at once, and nobody asks for a source.

options.text: Check only the posts I disagree with
options.then: You check only the posts you doubt, and the flattering ones pass.

options.text: Ask friends who think like me
options.then: They all agree, which feels like proof and is only the same view again.

steps.why: Agreeing makes you less likely to check, so decode the flattering claims too.

steps.prompt: You look for the other side of the story. Where do you go?

options.text: A few sources with different views
options.then: You read three. Two disagree, and you can see what each leaves out.

options.text: Only the first posts my feed shows me
options.then: The feed shows more of what you already believe.

options.text: The comments that agree with me
options.then: They agree warmly. You learn nothing new.

options.text: A page that mocks the other side
options.then: It is written to make you laugh, not to explain.

steps.why: You cannot weigh views you never see. Seek out others on purpose.

steps.prompt: A week later, a friend shows you a fact that only partly fits your view. What do you do?

options.text: Update my view, and say so if I shared it
options.then: You post a short note. A friend replies, "I should do that too."

options.text: Ignore the new facts and keep my view
options.then: The belief stays as it was, and so do the gaps in it.

options.text: Decide all sources are biased and stop reading
options.then: You stop reading anything, and your view gets even less checked.

options.text: Keep my view and unfollow whoever corrected me
options.then: Your feed gets quieter, and agrees with you more.

steps.why: Updating your view when the facts change is a strength, not a weakness.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder works hardest on the claims that flatter your existing view.
scenarios.relearn: Decode claims you agree with too; agreement isn't verification.

scenarios.hook: Your friend fell for a fake that you spotted straight away.

steps.prompt: They ask how you managed to avoid it. What do you say?

options.text: Walk them through the Decoder questions
options.then: You go through them on the fake together. They write the questions down.

options.text: Say I just got lucky
options.then: They nod. "So nothing to learn then."

options.text: Say it was obvious and they should have known
options.then: They feel foolish, and stop asking.

options.text: Say it is too long to explain
options.then: They shrug. "Okay. Never mind then."

steps.why: The Decoder is a learnable habit, so teach it kindly rather than call it luck.

steps.prompt: A day later, they ask for one thing to check first when a post shows up. What do you say?

options.text: Start with who made it and why
options.then: They try it on the fake. "It was an ad. I see it now."

options.text: Whether it looks real
options.then: They shake their head. "But this one looked real."

options.text: How many people shared it
options.then: They frown. "Everyone shared it, though."

options.text: Whether I like the person who posted it
options.then: They laugh. "So I would believe all my friends."

steps.why: Who made it and why comes first, before the look or the shares.

steps.prompt: A week later they try it on a new post and ask you to check. What do you do?

options.text: Look together and let them do the checking
options.then: They find the source themselves. They look pleased.

options.text: Do it for them quickly
options.then: The answer comes fast. They learn nothing new.

options.text: Tell them it is right without looking
options.then: They believe you, and the post was false.

options.text: Tell them to ask someone else
options.then: They leave it, and the habit does not stick.

steps.why: Letting them do the checking is how the habit passes on.

scenarios.debrief: Passing the Decoder on turns one decoder into many.
scenarios.relearn: The Decoder is a learnable habit you can teach, not luck.

scenarios.hook: An app nags you with a fake red badge to open it.

steps.prompt: A red badge shows 1, but there is nothing new inside. What do you do?

options.text: Name the hook, and open it only when I choose
options.then: You leave it unopened for now. The badge sits there, and you stay calm.

options.text: Open it right away because the badge says 1
options.then: There is nothing new, and you scroll for ten minutes anyway.

options.text: Open it just to clear the badge
options.then: The badge clears. Another one appears an hour later.

options.text: Check it every few minutes in case it changes
options.then: The badge never changes, and you lose half an hour glancing at your phone.

steps.why: A badge is attention-capture design. Naming it lets you choose when to open.

steps.prompt: More apps send badges and pings all day. What do you do?

options.text: Turn off non-essential notifications
options.then: The day gets quieter. Calls and family messages still come through.

options.text: Delete all my apps to be free of them
options.then: You feel free for a day, then miss your friends and the things you use.

options.text: Keep every notification on so I miss nothing
options.then: The pings keep coming, and you check your phone more than you meant to.

options.text: Turn off every alert, even calls from family
options.then: It is quiet, but you miss a call from your family.

steps.why: Turning off non-essential pings keeps what matters and drops the hooks.

steps.prompt: A friend says the pings make them feel anxious. What do you say?

options.text: The pings are designed to pull us back. Try muting some
options.then: They try it. "Oh. It is so much calmer already."

options.text: Just ignore them
options.then: They try, but the badge still catches their eye.

options.text: You are too sensitive about it
options.then: They stop sharing how they feel with you.

options.text: It is normal. Nothing you can do about it
options.then: They sigh, and keep checking all evening.

steps.why: The pull is by design, not a weakness. Muting some pings takes back the choice.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder applies to your own apps: name the hook, then choose.
scenarios.relearn: Name the design hook and use the app on purpose, not on its cue.

scenarios.hook: A "doctor" account sells a supplement that "fixes everything".

steps.prompt: The account's video ends with a link to buy it. What do you do?

options.text: Ask who benefits and check the account
options.then: The account names no hospital, and every video ends with a sale link.

options.text: Buy it, since a doctor would not lie online
options.then: You order it. Nothing in the video was checked.

options.text: Buy one bottle to see if it works
options.then: One bottle arrives, with no way to tell if it did anything.

options.text: Ask the comments if it worked for them
options.then: Several praise it. Some of those accounts were made last week.

steps.why: Ask who benefits. A costume and a sale link are not proof.

steps.prompt: You want to check whether the person is a real doctor. How?

options.text: Look for a named hospital or a medical registration
options.then: None of that is there, only a photo in a white coat.

options.text: Trust the white coat and the title in the bio
options.then: You trust the title. Later you find other sellers using the same one.

options.text: Check how many followers they have
options.then: The number is huge, and some of those followers may not be real.

options.text: Ask the account itself if it is a doctor
options.then: It says yes, and sends the sale link again.

steps.why: A real doctor can be traced to a hospital or a registry. A white coat can be posed in.

steps.prompt: A relative wants to buy it for a health problem. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest asking their own doctor before buying
options.then: They agree, and book an appointment.

options.text: Tell them it is a scam, full stop
options.then: They feel dismissed, and quietly buy it anyway.

options.text: Let them buy it, since it is their money
options.then: They buy it, and no one has checked it.

options.text: Buy it for them, to be kind
options.then: You feel generous, and the doubts stay unanswered.

steps.why: A real doctor who knows their health is the right check, and you can offer to go along.

scenarios.debrief: 'Who benefits?' cuts through a costume; the Decoder checks the account, not the look.
scenarios.relearn: Ask who benefits; a white-coat look online isn't proof.

scenarios.hook: You have decoded a post and it checks out as true.

steps.prompt: The post is accurate and useful. What do you do next?

options.text: Decide how to act on it, calmly and on purpose
options.then: You save it and decide to mention it to your class tomorrow.

options.text: Stop at "it is true" and do nothing with it
options.then: The post is forgotten, and nothing changes.

options.text: Share it with everyone without a note
options.then: Some reshare without reading, and the context gets lost.

options.text: Doubt it again, just to be sure
options.then: You re-check for an hour, and the answer stays the same.

steps.why: The last step is how you will act. Decoding ends in a decision, not a shrug.

steps.prompt: A friend says the post "proves" more than it actually says. What do you do?

options.text: Point out what it says and what it does not
options.then: Your friend rereads it. "Oh. It says less than I thought."

options.text: Agree, since the post is true after all
options.then: The stretched version spreads, with your agreement behind it.

options.text: Tell them they are wrong to think so
options.then: They feel brushed off, and keep thinking it.

options.text: Let them believe it
options.then: The bigger claim goes round the class, unchecked.

steps.why: A true post can still be stretched. Decode what it actually says.

steps.prompt: A week later, a new accurate post lands. You could ignore it, share it or act on it. How do you choose?

options.text: Ask what it really asks of me, then choose
options.then: You decide it asks for nothing, and you simply keep the fact.

options.text: Do whatever most people are doing
options.then: The class does what is easiest, and you go along with it.

options.text: Do whatever gets the quickest reaction
options.then: The reaction comes, and the point goes missing.

options.text: Pick the same option as last time
options.then: The last choice does not fit this time, and you only notice later.

steps.why: Choosing on purpose, based on what the post asks of you, finishes the Decoder.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder's final move is your own deliberate action.
scenarios.relearn: The Decoder ends with how you'll act, your decision, not just 'it's true'.

scenarios.hook: A new app demands access to your contacts and location.

steps.prompt: It will not continue until you answer. What do you do?

options.text: Decode the ask, and grant only what it needs
options.then: It works without either, so you tap Don't allow and it opens fine.

options.text: Tap allow on both so it stops asking
options.then: The app keeps using both until you change the setting.

options.text: Tap allow on both and check settings later
options.then: Later never comes, and it uses both every day.

options.text: Delete it, since every app is a trap
options.then: You miss the class chat that runs on it.

steps.why: Question the ask and grant the minimum.

steps.prompt: Later, an app asks for your camera, microphone and photos. What do you do?

options.text: Allow only what a feature needs, when I use it
options.then: You allow the camera for one photo. It asks again next time.

options.text: Allow all three to save time
options.then: The app now has access to all three, even when you are not using it.

options.text: Refuse all three and stop using its features
options.then: The app barely works, so you stop using it.

options.text: Ask a friend to allow it for me
options.then: Your friend allows everything, and you never see what it can reach.

steps.why: Granting each permission only when a feature needs it keeps control with you.

steps.prompt: A week later, your settings show an app using your location all day. What do you do?

options.text: Change the setting to only while using the app
options.then: The app still works, and far less of your location is shared.

options.text: Leave it, since it is already allowed
options.then: It keeps using your location, and you forget about it.

options.text: Ignore it, since I have nothing to hide
options.then: It keeps tracking, and you never ask why it needs to.

options.text: Turn off location on the whole phone for good
options.then: Your maps stop working, and you turn it back on in a week.

steps.why: You can always change a permission later. Check what each app really needs.

scenarios.debrief: The Decoder applies to permissions: question the ask, grant the minimum.
scenarios.relearn: Decode permission asks; grant only the data truly needed.

scenarios.hook: You want to make decoding automatic, not a chore.

steps.prompt: You have ten spare minutes on the bus. What do you do?

options.text: Run the Decoder on a few ordinary posts
options.then: You check a recipe and a meme. By the third, it takes seconds.

options.text: Save it for a big, important post
options.then: No big post comes that day, and the habit goes unpractised.

options.text: Read about the Decoder instead of using it
options.then: You know the steps, and have not yet used them on a real post.

options.text: Scroll for fun and decode later

steps.prompt: A week later, you think about decoding again, and it feels like a chore. What do you do?

options.text: Make it tiny: one question on one post a day
options.then: It takes five seconds, and you keep it up all week.

options.text: Quit, since it is too much work
options.then: The habit fades, and a misleading post slips by.

options.text: Do it for an hour in one go on Sunday
options.then: The hour is dull, and you skip the next Sunday.

options.text: Only decode posts that annoy me
options.then: You catch the annoying ones, and miss the ones that please you.

steps.why: A tiny daily check lasts longer than a big occasional one.

steps.prompt: A big viral claim spreads at school. How do you react?

options.text: Pause on reflex, then check the source
options.then: You stop before anyone shares it and ask who made it.

options.text: Share it before the others do
options.then: You post first, and later find it was a hoax.

options.text: Go along with the class, since they are mostly right
options.then: The class repeats it, and a few believe it.

options.text: Say the Decoder is too slow for this
options.then: You skip it, and the claim fools half the class.

steps.why: Daily reps on ordinary posts make the pause a reflex when it matters.

scenarios.debrief: Daily reps on ordinary posts turn the Decoder into a reflex for life.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two signs a 'giveaway' account is a scam.

scene.text: Links only to its official, named site
Asks for your OTP to 'confirm'
Never asks for passwords or codes
A near-copy handle with an extra letter
Has a long, consistent posting history

scenarios.why: Asking for your OTP and a copycat handle are scam signs; the rest are normal and safe.
scenarios.relearn: OTP requests and copycat handles are scam signs; never share codes, report via 1930.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two habits that keep you in a filter bubble.

scene.text: Following a few accounts you disagree with
Only watching what's served to you
Reading past the first opinion you meet
Blocking every view you don't like
Searching out a topic on purpose

scenarios.why: Only watching what's fed to you and blocking all other views harden the bubble; the rest open it.
scenarios.relearn: Deliberately seek other views; you can't weigh what you're never shown.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the Decoder is five small questions you can run on anything. Ready to own it?
scenarios.affirm: Five small questions, run on anything, are yours to keep for life.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: think of the last thing that made you want to instantly share. Picture pausing first.

scenarios.relearn: Build in a short pause; decoding beats reacting in a hurry.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the Decoder doesn't make you cynical, it makes you clear.

scenarios.relearn: Learning never stops; decoding is a habit for life.

scenarios.hook: A scary "breaking news" clip is doing the rounds in your class.
scenarios.setup: Your friend Nisha has her thumb over the send button.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "This is so scary. I am sending it to everyone."

options.text: "Wait. Let us check the source before we send it."
options.then: She pauses. "Okay. But it feels urgent."

options.text: "Just send it. It is probably fine anyway."
options.then: She sends it to six groups at once.

options.text: "Send it, but tell them all to be careful."
options.then: She adds a warning, and still sends it to everyone.

options.text: "Go ahead. Better they know than not at all."
options.then: She sends it, and a dozen replies come back at once.

steps.why: Fakes spread fastest when a scary clip is forwarded before it is checked.

steps.prompt: Nisha asks: "If it is real, people need to know. How do we tell?"

options.text: "Real news will have it too. Let us look."
options.then: She searches. "Hm. Nothing from any real news page yet."

options.text: "Sending fast is the kind thing to do either way."
options.then: She nods and forwards it to a group.

options.text: "Do not bother. They will find out anyway."
options.then: She shrugs and puts the phone down, the clip still going round.

options.text: "It is not your job to check."
options.then: She frowns. "Whose job is it, then?"

steps.why: A real event will show up on trusted news too. Checking costs a minute.

steps.prompt: Nisha says: "A friend just told me no news page has it. Now what?"

options.text: "Hold it, and tell anyone who has it that it is unconfirmed."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. I will message them now."

options.text: "Send it anyway. You never know what is true."
options.then: She sends it, and the clip travels further.

options.text: "Delete it and never mention it again to anyone."
options.then: She deletes it, and the friends who sent it never find out.

options.text: "Keep it saved in case it turns out to be true."
options.then: She keeps it saved, and the clip keeps spreading without her.

steps.why: Without a source, hold it. Telling others it is unconfirmed keeps it from spreading.

scenarios.relearn: Ask to verify the source before forwarding a scary clip.

scenarios.hook: Your younger cousin Yash is new to watching videos and posts online.
scenarios.setup: He asks it while the two of you wait for the bus.

steps.prompt: Yash asks: "How do you tell what is real online?"

options.text: "I ask who made it, why, and if it is true."
options.then: He repeats it. "Who, why, true. Okay."

options.text: "You just kind of know after some time online."
options.then: He looks puzzled. "But how will I know?"

options.text: "If it looks real enough, it usually is real."
options.then: He nods, and believes the next good-looking video.

options.text: "I only trust whatever my friends send."
options.then: He grins. "That is easy. They send me everything."

steps.why: Teach the three questions plainly. A feeling is not something he can copy.

steps.prompt: Yash shows you a viral video and asks: "Who even makes these? How do I find out?"

options.text: "Tap the account and see who they are."
options.then: He taps. "It is a page that only sells things."

options.text: "Check how many followers they have."
options.then: He nods. "A million. So it is true."

options.text: "Ask the comments."
options.then: Several agree, and none can say who made it.

options.text: "Do not bother. Most posts have no author."
options.then: He sighs. "So I cannot know anything?"

steps.why: The account tells you who made it and why. Followers do not.

steps.prompt: Yash says: "What if I check and still cannot tell?"

options.text: "Then I wait and ask someone I trust."
options.then: He relaxes. "So I do not have to decide right now."

options.text: "Then go with your gut."
options.then: He shrugs. "My gut says yes."

options.text: "Then share it so others can decide."
options.then: He shares it, and now the others are stuck with the same doubt.

options.text: "Then it is probably false."
options.then: He frowns. "But sometimes true things are hard to check."

steps.why: Waiting and asking someone you trust is a valid result of decoding.

scenarios.relearn: Teach the Decoder simply: who made it, why, and is it true?

scenarios.hook: A relative shares a "cure" and asks why you look unsure.
scenarios.setup: Your uncle waves his phone at you.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Why that face? This herbal cure works for everything."

options.text: "I would love to check it with a doctor first. Can we?"
options.then: He pauses. "A doctor? Hm. I will think about it."

options.text: "You are right. Let us just believe it."
options.then: He beams, and sends the cure to the whole family.

options.text: "That is rubbish. You should not believe everything."
options.then: He stiffens. "I have been around longer than you."

options.text: "Maybe. I do not know enough to say."
options.then: He nods, and takes it as agreement.

steps.why: Kindly asking to check with a doctor keeps respect and gets a real answer.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "My neighbour swears by it and says doctors only want to sell medicines. This is natural."

options.text: "Natural does not mean checked. A doctor can say what is safe."
options.then: He thinks. "Safe for me, you mean. Hm."

options.text: "You may be right. Doctors do earn money."
options.then: He nods. "Exactly. I knew you would see it."

options.text: "Then ask the seller of the cure."
options.then: He calls the seller, who says it is perfectly safe.

options.text: "Fine. Try the cure along with your medicine."
options.then: He starts both, and no one has asked whether they mix.

steps.why: A doctor can say what is safe for him, which a seller or a label cannot.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "I have a check-up with my doctor on Saturday. Will you come along?"

options.text: "Yes. I will come, and we will ask about it together."
options.then: He smiles. "Good. I will not feel silly, then."

options.text: "I am busy. Go on your own."
options.then: He shrugs, and goes without asking about the cure.

options.text: "No. It is your health, so your decision."
options.then: He nods, and buys the cure on the way home.

options.text: "Yes, but we will not tell the doctor about the cure."
options.then: He agrees, and the doctor never hears about it.

steps.why: Going along with him respects him, and gets him real answers.

scenarios.relearn: Verify a health claim with a doctor before trusting it.

scenarios.hook: A friend is furious at an outrage post and wants you to pile on.
scenarios.setup: Her messages arrive one after another, all in capitals.

steps.prompt: Rhea texts: "Can you BELIEVE this? Let us blast them!"

options.text: "Let us pause. Who gains if we get this angry?"
options.then: She replies. "Hm. The page, I guess. It gets the clicks."

options.text: "Yeah, let us go and blast them properly."
options.then: She sends back a fire emoji and drafts a harsh reply.

options.text: "Calm down. It is only one post, honestly."
options.then: She types in capitals. "It is NOT only a post."

options.text: "Let us share it first and think later."
options.then: She shares it. It spreads before either of you checks it.

steps.why: Engineered outrage wants an instant share. A pause breaks it.

steps.prompt: Rhea asks: "Is it wrong to be this angry at something like this?"

options.text: "Be angry. Just check it is true first."
options.then: She exhales. "Fine. Let me check."

options.text: "Yes. Anger is silly. Do not feel it."
options.then: She stiffens. "Do not tell me how to feel."

options.text: "You can be angry, but keep it to yourself."
options.then: She frowns. "Why should I hide it?"

options.text: "They deserve it, so go ahead."
options.then: She posts the harshest one yet.

steps.why: No feeling is bad. Checking before you act is what keeps the anger from using you.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "A friend checked, and half of that post is made up. Now what?"

options.text: "Share the true part, name the twist."
options.then: She posts the clearer version. "That feels better."

options.text: "Delete it and say nothing."
options.then: She deletes it, and others keep sharing the twisted version.

options.text: "Blast them for lying, then."
options.then: She goes back in angrier, and the thread blows up.

options.text: "Never mind. It was only a post."
options.then: She shrugs, and the half-truth stays out there.

steps.why: Sharing the true part and naming the twist stops the outrage from spreading.

scenarios.relearn: Pause and ask who benefits from your anger before sharing.

scenarios.hook: A friend got an "OTP to claim your prize" message and is about to reply.
scenarios.setup: She holds up her phone, grinning.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "I won a prize! I just reply with the OTP, right?"

options.text: "Do not share the OTP. No real prize needs it."
options.then: She frowns. "But it says I will lose the prize."

options.text: "Go on, send it so you do not lose the prize."
options.then: She starts typing it in, then stops. "Wait. My bank said never to share this."

options.text: "Send it, but ask them who they are first."
options.then: They reply with a link and ask again for the OTP.

options.text: "Ask your friends if they got one too."
options.then: Two have the same message, and nobody knows what it is.

steps.why: Anyone who needs your OTP for a prize is running the scam.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "I still do not know. The message looks so official, with a logo."

options.text: "Logos are easy to copy. Check the company's own app."
options.then: She opens the company's own app. "No prize is mentioned."

options.text: "True, it looks official. It is probably a real prize."
options.then: She nods, then frowns. "But why would it need my OTP, then?"

options.text: "Then reply to the message and ask them for proof first."
options.then: They send a fake certificate, and push harder for the OTP.

options.text: "Then ignore it and forget it. It is only a message."
options.then: She ignores it. The message sits there, unreported, and nobody else knows about it.

steps.why: Logos and certificates are easy to fake. Checking the company's own app is the test.

steps.prompt: Kavya asks: "Okay. Who do I tell about this?"

options.text: "Tell a parent or trusted adult, and report it on cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. We can report it together tonight."

options.text: "Nobody. It is a bit embarrassing, so keep it quiet."
options.then: She keeps it to herself. Nobody reports it and no adult knows.

options.text: "Just block the number and move on. That is enough."
options.then: She blocks it. The scam goes on to the next person.

options.text: "Message the sender back to say you know their trick."
options.then: They answer with new links and fresh threats.

steps.why: Reporting via cybercrime 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in helps stop it for others, and nobody is at fault for being targeted.

scenarios.relearn: Never share an OTP; no genuine prize needs it.

scenarios.hook: You shared a post yesterday, and your friend Sameer has been checking it.
scenarios.setup: He shows you the debunked post on his phone.

steps.prompt: Sameer says: "Hey, the post you shared yesterday was false."

options.text: "You are right. Thanks. I will post a correction."
options.then: He relaxes. "Good. I thought you would be upset."

options.text: "I will just quietly delete it."
options.then: He nods slowly. "People already saw it, though."

options.text: "It was not my fault. I got it from someone else."
options.then: He raises his eyebrows. "You still shared it."

options.text: "Everyone shares stuff like that. It is no big deal."
options.then: He shrugs. "People did believe it, though."

steps.why: Thanking him and correcting openly is repair without shame.

steps.prompt: Sameer asks: "People are still sharing it. What should they hear about it?"

options.text: "That it was false, and what tell I missed."
options.then: He nods. "That helps other people spot it too."

options.text: "Just that I am sorry, with no other details."
options.then: He tilts his head. "Sorry for what, though?"

options.text: "That it was only a joke."
options.then: He frowns. "You shared it as if it were real."

options.text: "That the page I got it from lied."
options.then: He shrugs. "That does not tell them what to look for."

steps.why: A clear correction says what was false and what the tell was.

steps.prompt: Sameer says: "A few people are teasing you about it. How will you handle it?"

options.text: "I will own it, name the tell, and tell someone if it stings."
options.then: He grins. "Okay. That takes the sting out of it."

options.text: "I will argue with each of them in the comments."
options.then: He winces. "That will keep it going for days."

options.text: "I will get back at them."
options.then: He sighs. "That will just make it bigger."

options.text: "I will say they have shared fake things too."
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "True. But that changes nothing for you."

steps.why: Owning a slip lightly, and learning the tell, is how repair finishes. No shame.

scenarios.relearn: Correct a false share openly and thank the person who flagged it.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Pooja is doubtful about decoding what she sees online.
scenarios.setup: She sighs as you describe the Decoder.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "Decoding everything sounds exhausting. And so cynical."

options.text: "It is not cynicism. It is a quick, kind check."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "A quick check? That is not so bad."

options.text: "Yeah. Maybe it is honestly not worth the effort."
options.then: She nods, relieved, then hesitates. "But you do check some things, right?"

options.text: "Cynical is smart. Trust nobody online at all."
options.then: She laughs. "That sounds even more exhausting."

options.text: "You just do not want to learn it."
options.then: She stiffens. "I did not say that."

steps.why: A quick check keeps you both sharp and kind. It is not cynicism.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "So when do you actually decode, and when do you let it go?"

options.text: "Only what I might share or act on."
options.then: She nods. "So only the ones that matter."

options.text: "Every post, every time."
options.then: She groans. "See? Exhausting."

options.text: "Only the ones I disagree with."
options.then: She tilts her head. "So your own side never gets checked?"

options.text: "Only the ones everyone is talking about."
options.then: She shrugs. "That is only the loud ones."

steps.why: You decode what you might share or act on, not every single post.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "Does it make you trust people less?"

options.text: "No. I check the post and stay kind to people."
options.then: She smiles. "That sounds almost relaxing."

options.text: "Yes. Everyone online is out for something."
options.then: She wrinkles her nose. "That is bleak."

options.text: "Yes, and that is fine."
options.then: She frowns. "I would not want to live like that."

options.text: "Not at all. I never doubt anything."
options.then: She laughs. "That is not what you said."

steps.why: Critical, not cynical: question the post, and keep your trust in people.

scenarios.relearn: Decoding is a quick, kind check, not cynicism or hard work.

myth.un: "If it's trending, it must be true."

myth.why: Virality tracks emotional or engineered spread, which isn't the same as truth.
